Qualcomm on track to bring first Wi-Fi 8 products to market by end-2026
Qualcomm plans to launch its first Wi-Fi 8 products by late 2026, enhancing network reliability, capacity, and latency with AI-powered gateways and advanced multi-antenna technology for improved connectivity.
The company is also working on network anomaly detection, troubleshooting and security applications. (Image/X)
Qualcomm is on track to bring its initial Wi-Fi 8 products to market towards the end of 2026, with the rollout expected to expand thereafter, according to a senior company executive.
Gautam Sheoran, Senior Vice President and General Manager, Connectivity, Broadband & Networking, Qualcomm told FE that the company is working with major OEM partners, including several existing Wi-Fi 7 partners, on the transition to Wi-Fi 8.
Trai allows two-way communication on 1600 series
“Wi-Fi 8 is going to start at the end of this year with the most aggressive device makers, and then it’s going to expand in the next year,” he said.
The technology is designed to improve network reliability, increase capacity and reduce latency, particularly as connected devices increasingly support simultaneous applications such as gaming, video streaming, remote work and Internet of Things (IoT) services.
Qualcomm is additionally integrating artificial intelligence engines into network gateways to classify applications and traffic, allowing networks to prioritise bandwidth and maintain quality of service for latency-sensitive applications. The company is also working on network anomaly detection, troubleshooting and security applications.
“Every house has a gateway that provides you internet access. And that’s typically been a black box or a white box, getting data in, sending data out, not a lot of intelligence,” Sheoran said, adding that this is an area where the company expects rapid change.
The shift towards intelligent gateways is particularly relevant as consumers use multiple connected devices simultaneously, mainly for cloud gaming, where delays in network response can affect the user experience.
Imprint of price rejig, user churn likely on telcos quarter
Sheoran added that for the first time, Qualcomm is putting a 4×4 Wi-Fi radio in its handset chips. It is also launching what it calls the industry’s first 5×5 radio for access points. The extra antennas extend range and improve stability. The chips integrate AI engines that prioritise traffic, so that gaming, work calls and streaming do not compete in busy homes. The company has also worked on cutting power consumption, he added.
On top of this sits Qualcomm’s Dragonwing Network AI suite, which classifies traffic, applications and devices, Sheoran said that the firm seeks to develop in-home sensing and security features. “Edge security, especially in the gateways, is going to become more and more important,” Sheoran said, adding that hacking is getting easier.
India is major base for Qualcomm’s chip and software development, Sheoran said, calling the talent base and the volume of work as extremely integral.

Recent reporting about thermal issues related to Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 is inaccurate. We are proud of the innovation and strong momentum behind our next-generation flagship platform and continue to work closely with global OEMs to deliver premium user experiences.

There are no systemic thermal issues with the 8 elite gen 6. OEMs are consistently tuning their platforms as they launch their products. Always trying to balance performance and power to optimize their value props around different use cases. We work together to deliver the best…

Can Qualcomm's PickNik Acquisition Strengthen Its Robotics Edge?
Tue, October 20, 2026 at 8:09 AM CDT 2 min read
Qualcomm Incorporated QCOM is strengthening its position in the rapidly evolving robotics market through its proposed acquisition of PickNik Robotics, a developer of advanced robotics software. The transaction aligns with Qualcomm's strategy to expand its footprint in physical artificial intelligence (AI), edge computing and intelligent robotics.
PickNik is recognized for its stewardship of MoveIt, a widely adopted open-source robotics manipulation framework built on the Robot Operating System (ROS). The platform supports motion planning, manipulation and robotic control across industrial automation, service robotics and emerging physical AI applications. The transaction, subject to customary closing conditions, could strengthen Qualcomm's ability to offer integrated hardware and software solutions.
The buyout is expected to enhance Qualcomm's Dragonwing Robotics platforms by integrating MoveIt and PickNik's commercial MoveIt Pro software. This combination could enable developers to leverage Qualcomm's AI processing, connectivity and heterogeneous computing capabilities alongside advanced motion planning and real-time robotic control.
The integration is also expected to extend to Arduino platforms, beginning with VENTUNO Q boards. This could make advanced robotics development more accessible to a broader developer community while accelerating the transition from prototypes to commercial deployments.
Importantly, Qualcomm intends to maintain MoveIt as an open-source framework supporting third-party hardware. This approach could encourage wider ecosystem participation and strengthen developer engagement, potentially boosting adoption of its Dragonwing platforms.
Physical AI Opportunities Support Long-Term Diversification
The planned acquisition complements Qualcomm's broader efforts to diversify beyond smartphones into automotive, industrial IoT and edge AI markets. Its March 2026 collaboration with NEURA Robotics to advance cognitive robotics and humanoid applications further underscores its growing focus on physical AI.
Combining PickNik's software expertise with Qualcomm's power-efficient computing capabilities could improve its competitive positioning as demand for intelligent automation increases across industrial and commercial applications.
However, the acquisition's financial terms remain undisclosed, limiting visibility into its immediate earnings contribution. Integration challenges, competition in robotics computing and uncertain commercialization timelines could also constrain near-term benefits. Stiff competition from NVIDIA Corporation NVDA, Broadcom Inc. AVGO and Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. AMD further strains its margins.
Nevertheless, PickNik's established developer ecosystem and robotics software capabilities could help Qualcomm expand its addressable market and deepen customer engagement. Successful integration may strengthen QCOM's position in next-generation robotics while supporting its long-term diversification strategy.

Prediction: Qualcomm Could Be on the Verge of a Major Transformation
Qualcomm is entering data center and automotive markets at full speed while Apple shrinks its handset business and analysts pile on with downward revisions. Whether those new revenue streams arrive fast enough to fill the gap will decide everything for…
Published October 5, 2026, 8:45am ET · 3 min read
Price Targets desk. Editor: Vandita Jadeja.
The 24/7 Wall St. price target for Qualcomm (NASDAQ:QCOM | QCOM Price Prediction) is $218.04 over the next 12 months. From a reference price of $184.1, that works out to 18.44% upside, and our model rates the stock a buy.
Price Target from 24/7 Wall St.
Management targets $40 billion in non-handset revenue by fiscal 2029, up from $22 billion. Non-handset growth is expected to speed up from 24% in fiscal 2026 to greater than 60% in fiscal 2027. If Qualcomm delivers, the business will look very different by decade’s end.
Qualcomm Has Pulled Back Hard From Its June Peak
The stock is down 6.01% over the past week. It is still up 14.12% over the past month and 10.67% year to date. Qualcomm underperformed its competitors on Monday. Shares trade about 28.5% below their 52-week high of $257.56 and about 52.3% above their low of $120.88.
In fiscal Q3, revenue came in at $9.947 billion, ahead of the $9.672 billion estimate. Non-GAAP EPS of $2.21 narrowly missed expectations. Handset revenue fell 20%, while automotive revenue rose 61% to $1.588 billion.
Why Bulls See Data Center Revenue Rewriting the Story
Two custom silicon deals with hyperscalers begin revenue in the December quarter. Management targets $5 billion in fiscal 2027 and $15 billion in fiscal 2029 for data center.
The AI expansion reaches well beyond the accelerator makers, and we featured seven of the less-obvious infrastructure suppliers in a free report you can grab here.
In automotive, Qualcomm raised its annualized revenue target to about $7 billion and won the lead compute supplier role for BMW’s next-generation ADAS and digital cockpit. The most optimistic fiscal 2027 EPS estimate is $12.24. Our bull case of $237.62 implies about 29% upside.
Apple’s Exit and Margin Pressure Could Stall the Rerating
Management expects Apple product revenue to fall about 50% from September to December. Over the past 30 days, analysts made 27 downward revisions to fiscal 2027 estimates.
Consensus EPS for fiscal 2027 now stands at $10.1772, below the $10.4834 expected for fiscal 2026. Custom data center chips could cut QCT gross margin by 1.5% to 2%.
Qualcomm is raising prices by double-digit amounts to offset higher costs. In the bear case of $185.27, the stock stays about flat over 12 months.
Qualcomm Trades Below Its Custom Silicon Rivals
Broadcom (NASDAQ:AVGO) leads the hyperscaler custom silicon market that Qualcomm is entering. It trades at nearly the same forward multiple while growing revenue 85.5%.
Marvell (NASDAQ:MRVL) shows what investors pay once a custom silicon ramp is proven: a forward multiple of 62x.
Texas Instruments (NASDAQ:TXN) is a useful comparison for automotive and industrial chips, and it trades at 28x. Against this group, the 24/7 Wall St. price target looks conservative.
Qualcomm’s Transformation Tips the Balance Toward Upside
The 24/7 Wall St. price target is $218.04, with a buy rating and 90% confidence. Qualcomm trades at a peer-level multiple while data center revenue is only now coming.
Upside hinges on hyperscaler shipments starting on schedule in December and price increases restoring margins. On the downside, Android weakness could compound the Apple decline.
These year-end targets assume Qualcomm keeps executing its current strategy.
Price Target from 24/7 Wall St.
The biggest swing factor is data center execution. Hitting the $15 billion fiscal 2029 target would push results above this path, and a delayed accelerator launch would pull them below it.

Qualcomm Stock Climbs as Report Reveals Possible November Layoffs
Tue, October 20, 2026 at 8:02 AM CDT 1 min read
This article first appeared on GuruFocus.
Qualcomm (NASDAQ:QCOM) shares rose 1% Tuesday morning after a report said the chipmaker plans to reduce its workforce following annual employee reviews in November, according to Reuters.
Chief Executive Cristiano Amon outlined a performance-focused reduction in a memo sent to employees, Reuters reported, citing the internal communication. The report did not provide a potential job-cut figure or identify the business units that could be affected.

The planned workforce changes are expected to follow Qualcomm's November review process. However, the available report did not clarify whether the reductions would involve employees across the company or focus on particular departments.
The report also did not specify whether Qualcomm expects the cuts to generate cost savings or provide an estimate of their potential financial impact. Details about the timing of any employee departures were not included.
Qualcomm has not provided a public figure for the proposed reduction in the information cited by Reuters. The scale of the cuts and the number of employees potentially affected therefore remain uncertain as the company approaches its annual evaluations.

Qualcomm To Reportedly Conduct Global Layoffs In Performance-Driven Overhaul
Tue, October 20, 2026 at 1:07 PM CDT 2 min read
Qualcomm CEO Cristiano Amon announced the worldwide job cuts in an internal memo, with individual notifications scheduled to begin in November.
Although the exact magnitude of the layoffs has not been disclosed, the firm reported a global headcount of approximately 52,000 employees as of last September.
The downsizing coincides with ongoing consumer electronics slumps and a strategic corporate transition toward artificial intelligence data-center expansion.
Qualcomm (QCOM) is preparing to downsize its global workforce through a performance-focused reduction strategy, Reuters reported on Tuesday.
In an internal company memo reviewed by Reuters on Monday, Chief Executive Officer Cristiano Amon informed staff that the upcoming personnel changes will follow after the completion of yearly employee performance evaluations.
See what 10M+ investors are talking about. Get the Stocktwits Daily Rip for what retail is watching right now, free to your inbox
Amon stated that the workforce adjustments are designed to build a robust performance culture and directly address instances where teams have consistently missed targets.
While the memo omitted specific figures regarding the total number of positions affected, public records indicate that Qualcomm maintained roughly 52,000 full-time global employees as of September of last year. Formal notifications regarding the cuts are slated to begin rolling out in November.
Qualcomm is among the world's leading smartphone chipmakers and is facing significant headwinds lately from a broader demand slump driven by soaring memory component prices.
Consequently, Qualcomm shares have experienced sluggish growth, rising just 1.5% in 2026, lagging significantly behind the broader S&P 500 and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index (SOX).
Amon emphasized that the restructuring process will carefully weigh current business priorities, required organizational competencies, and individual skill sets. "As we have expanded the business, so have the competencies and skills we require," Amon noted in the internal communication. "We must have the right people in the right roles so they can perform at their best and the company can continue to succeed."

On October 5, 2026, Qualcomm and Huawei announced a multi-year patent agreement covering 5G, compute, artificial intelligence and networking.
According to Huawei on October 5, 2026, the companies will cross-license their patent portfolios, while Qualcomm will purchase certain Huawei U.S. patents covering compute, artificial intelligence, networking and other technologies.
The transaction remains subject to regulatory approvals, and the companies disclosed no financial terms. Reuters reported on October 5, 2026, that the agreement is Huawei's first patent licensing deal with Qualcomm covering 5G and could lift Huawei's cumulative licensing contract value above USD 6.9 billion once completed.

The comparison shows a mixed earnings profile. Revenue exceeded the USD 9.69 billion estimate cited by MarketBeat, but earnings per share missed consensus by USD 0.02, leaving the licensing agreement as a strategic development rather than a quantified near-term earnings boost.
The primary-market quote was last at USD 180.79 on Nasdaq at 4:00 p.m. ET on October 5, 2026. Qualcomm's market capitalization was USD 189.8 billion on that date, while its 52-week range stood at USD 121.99 to USD 259.92.
The valuation context matters because the Huawei agreement has no disclosed purchase price or royalty schedule. Texas Instruments (TXN) To Report Earnings Tomorrow: Here Is What To Expect
Analog chip manufacturer Texas Instruments (NASDAQ:TXN) will be announcing earnings results this Wednesday after the bell. Here's what you need to know.
Texas Instruments beat analysts' revenue expectations last quarter, reporting revenues of $5.46 billion, up 22.8% year on year. It was an exceptional quarter for the company, with a beat of analysts' EPS and operating income estimates.
Is Texas Instruments a buy or sell going into earnings? Read our full analysis here, it's free for active Edge members.
This quarter, the market is expecting Texas Instruments's revenue to grow 24.4% year on year, improving from the 14.2% increase it recorded in the same quarter last year.
Analysts covering the company have generally reconfirmed their estimates over the last 30 days, suggesting they anticipate the business will stay the course heading into earnings. Texas Instruments rarely misses Wall Street's revenue estimates.
Looking at Texas Instruments's peers in the semiconductors segment, some have already reported their Q3 results, giving us a hint as to what we can expect. Penguin Solutions delivered year-on-year revenue growth of 67.7%, beating analysts' expectations by 8.8%, and Micron reported revenues up 379%, topping estimates by 6.4%. Penguin Solutions traded up 13.1% following the results while Micron was also up 3%.
Read our full analysis of Penguin Solutions's results here and Micron's results here.
Over the last year or so, investors' attention has moved from one major market theme to the next, spanning AI disruption and surging infrastructure investment to geopolitical tensions, interest rates, and the health of the broader economy. While some of the semiconductors stocks have shown solid performance in this choppy environment, the group has generally underperformed, with share prices down 7.8% on average over the last month. Texas Instruments is up 2.5% during the same time and is heading into earnings with an average analyst price target of $324.39 (compared to the current share price of $277.56).

Lam Research and Texas Instruments both report after the close on Wednesday, and each faces a different kind of pressure: one must prove AI equipment demand is still accelerating, while the other needs to show its industrial recovery has real…
Published October 20, 2026, 7:50am ET · 3 min read
Automated robotic arms meticulously assemble electronic components on an advanced manufacturing line, illustrating the high-tech production methods driving growth in the semiconductor industry, particularly for AI equipment and industrial applications. © Shutterstock
Two chip stocks from opposite ends of the industry report on Wednesday, October 21, after the market close. Lam Research (NASDAQ:LRCX | LRCX Price Prediction) has to show that AI equipment demand is still accelerating. Texas Instruments (NASDAQ:TXN) has to show that its industrial and auto rebound can last.
Texas Instruments hosts its call at 3:30 p.m. Central time (4:30 p.m. ET). Lam follows at 5:00 p.m. ET.
Texas Instruments Faces a Test of Its Own Guidance
Texas Instruments makes analog chips that handle real-world signals like power and temperature. It also makes embedded processors, the small control chips built into machines. On its prior earnings call, Texas Instruments said revenue rose 13% sequentially and 23% year over year. Industrial, data center, and automotive customers led the growth.
Texas Instruments guided third-quarter revenue to $5.65 billion to $6.15 billion and EPS to $2.23 to $2.57. The consensus EPS estimate of $2.42 falls inside that range, so the fourth-quarter outlook carries more weight. Management said industrial revenue remains below its 2022 peak and customer inventories have not been rebuilt. Auto demand picked up, led by electric vehicles and hybrids in China. Shares are up 59.2% year to date.
Lam Research Rides AI Demand Into Record Guidance
Lam sells deposition and etch tools, the machines that add and carve away thin layers of material on silicon wafers. On its prior earnings call, Lam said it delivered record revenue, operating margin, and earnings per share “as AI-driven demand continues to reshape the semiconductor industry,” positioning it for “a third consecutive year of outperformance in 2026.”
Lam guided September-quarter revenue to $8.1 billion, plus or minus $400 million, and EPS to $2.15 plus or minus $0.15. It also raised its 2026 forecast for wafer fab equipment spending (what the whole industry spends on chipmaking tools) to the low $150 billion range.
In an August 26 Bloomberg Businessweek report, Lam Research said its advanced packaging business is growing more than 70% year over year. Advanced packaging stacks memory and processor chips in three dimensions and wires them together, so AI hardware works like one large system. Lam shares are down 12.1% over the past week and up 59.0% year to date.
Consensus Points to Steep Year-Over-Year Gains
Jim Cramer described the demand picture on October 19, saying CPUs are “going to be in very short supply, which I think is absolutely true because Taiwan Semi can’t make all the ones that they have.” He added, “There’s tremendous demand, and there’s also an inability to build.” On October 9, he said, “Taiwan Semi controlled pretty much any chip stock.”
When chipmakers cannot build fast enough, they add factory capacity, and that means buying more deposition and etch tools from Lam. Lam said the industry remains meaningfully undersupplied, with several new fabs expected to come online by the end of 2027. The same buildout is pulling in power, cooling, and networking suppliers alongside the chipmakers. (We rounded up seven of those names in a free AI infrastructure report.)
What Each Company Must Prove on Wednesday
Texas Instruments needs a fourth-quarter outlook showing that industrial and automotive demand is still climbing. Lam needs revenue close to its $8.1 billion guidance and more detail on 2027, a year management already called a potentially strong setup.

The Zacks Analyst Blog Highlights Meta Platforms, Lam Research, Texas Instruments, Tesla, Netflix, Procter & Gamble and GE Aerospace
Tue, October 20, 2026 at 6:27 AM CDT 6 min read
Chicago, IL – October 20, 2026 – Zacks.com announces the list of stocks featured in the Analyst Blog. Every day the Zacks Equity Research analysts discuss the latest news and events impacting stocks and the financial markets. Stocks recently featured in the blog include: Meta Platforms META, Lam Research LRCX, Texas Instruments TXN, Tesla TSLA, Netflix NFLX, Procter & Gamble PG and GE Aerospace GE.
Here are highlights from Monday's Analyst Blog:
Q3 Earnings Reports Gear Up: Global Week Ahead
What happens across this Global Week Ahead?
· Q3 earnings season is shifting up a gear in the U.S., and
· Mainland China is about to deliver a deluge of macro data
· Giving febrile markets plenty more to ponder after the latest bouts of volatility in bonds and AI stocks
Elsewhere:
· Central bankers in Indonesia and Turkey have been given headaches by global index provider MSCI, while
· Voters in Brazil gear up to choose their next president
Next are Reuters' five world market themes, re-ordered for equity traders—
U.S. earnings season picks up in the coming days, with investors focused on Meta Platforms and other AI-focused companies as technology shares wobble.
Meta, due on Wednesday, is one of several hyper-scalers whose massive spending on AI data centers and infrastructure has been a big driver of investment.
With concerns mounting over financing for the AI buildout, investors want more detail on expected returns from those huge outlays.
Reports from semiconductor companies Lam Research and Texas Instruments will offer another view of the AI boom, as will results from Elon Musk's Tesla.
Other high-profile results in the coming days include Netflix, Procter & Gamble and GE Aerospace.
S&P500 earnings are expected to have climbed more than +30% in the third quarter, according to LSEG IBES, continuing a robust year for corporate profits.
(2) Stock & Bond Returns Correlation a Focus
For months, as energy and food prices surged amid the Iran war, bonds lost their shock-absorber status as investors jacked up estimates of how high interest rates might need to go.
Add near-chronic concern ‌about developed-world governments' finances, and bonds seemed to offer little safe-haven comfort while still struggling to rival super-charged equities.
The correlation between stocks and bond yields has now turned positive for Europe and the U.S., meaning yields are more likely to fall when stocks fall.
It had been overwhelmingly negative this year, with yields rising as stocks fell, undermining bonds' traditional role as a haven during equity selloffs.
This relationship fluctuates, but this year, the correlation of U.S. stocks and bond yields in March hit its most negative since at least the 1990s, while for European assets, it reached its most negative on record in September.
(3) MSCI Proposed Stripping Indonesia of EM Status. Turkey Put on Notice, Too
Central bankers in Indonesia and Turkey already have plenty on their plates.
Now they have an MSCI headache, too.
Indonesia's central bank meets on Wednesday, while Turkish policymakers gather on Thursday, against a backdrop of high energy prices, rising borrowing costs, AI-driven market disruption and geopolitical uncertainty.
MSCI has proposed stripping Indonesia of its emerging-market (EM) status and removing it from a suite of indexes, a move that risks triggering heavy outflows and raising pressure on policymakers to hike from 5.75% rather than hold.
MSCI has also put Turkey on notice, warning of a potential downgrade if market reforms fall short by mid-2027, another complication for policymakers expected to keep cutting rates from 37%.
(4) The Week Starts with a Mainland China Macro Data Deluge
A health check on the Chinese economy is due on Monday, with third-quarter GDP alongside September retail sales, industrial output and fixed-asset investment data.
The latest loan prime rate follows on Tuesday and is expected to stay put after more than a year on hold.
Strong global demand for semiconductors, clean technology and other manufactured goods has kept China's economy ticking, even as domestic demand remains patchy and higher energy costs bite.
Exports have held up despite China's delicate trade balancing act with the U.S. and E.U.
The latest trade figures showed Chinese exports surging well beyond analysts' estimates, putting the country on track for another $1 trillion trade surplus this year after crossing the threshold for the first time in 2025.
The flip side: the export boom could add to trade tensions with major partners.
(4) Brazil's Presidential Runoff Happens on October 25th. Campaigning Underway
Brazil's October 25th presidential runoff is keeping markets on edge after Flávio Bolsonaro's surprise first-round lead sent stocks up 7.7% and the real almost 4% higher.
A new Quaest poll puts Bolsonaro on 46% versus Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva's 44%, a technical tie.
Investors are betting a Bolsonaro win would bring tighter fiscal policy, but much may already be priced in. His choice of economic team and signs of credible reform could fuel further gains.
A Lula comeback, meanwhile, could put that rally into reverse, with the real, longer-dated bonds and state-controlled companies among the most exposed. A more conservative Congress, though, could limit how far Lula could shift policy.

Texas Instruments Incorporated (NASDAQ:TXN) stands out as a favorite among long-term dividend investors. The company's analog chips and embedded processors power everything from industrial machines and cars to data centers and home electronics. Because these products stick around for years, Texas Instruments enjoys steady repeat business and a real edge over competitors, thanks to its manufacturing know-how, engineering talent, and strong customer ties. These qualities also explain why the company often features in discussions of durable income-generating businesses, including Top 10 Unstoppable Dividend Stocks to Buy. Still, investors have to pay a premium for that kind of stability. Still, investors have to pay a premium for that kind of stability.
Texas Instruments' forward P/E is 27.55, while its trailing P/E sits much higher at 41.43. That gap shows investors expect earnings to bounce back from last year's lower numbers.

Texas Instruments: 3 Things to Watch Before Buying the Dividend Stock
1. Earnings recovery is real, but not risk-free
The most recent quarter backs up the idea that things are turning around. In Q2 2026, revenue jumped 23% year over year to $5.46 billion, and net income surged 53% to $1.98 billion. Operating profit also climbed 48% to $2.31 billion, pushing operating margins to about 42.3%. Strong demand from factories, data centers, and automakers drove those gains.
Cash flow got a boost too. Over the past year, Texas Instruments Incorporated (NASDAQ:TXN) generated $6.53 billion in free cash flow, though that total includes $1.18 billion from CHIPS Act incentives. That's important because manufacturing investments, depreciation, and when government incentives hit the books all play a role in how much cash is left for dividends and buybacks.
2. Forward P/E: better than the past, but not a bargain
At a forward P/E of 27.55, TXN now trades higher than its forward multiples of 25.58 at the end of 2025 and 26.25 in September 2025, according to Yahoo Finance. The even higher trailing P/E of 41.43 highlights just how much last year's earnings were weighed down compared to what's expected going forward.
That forward P/E means investors are getting an earnings yield of just 3.63%, not great when you compare it to the 5.2% yield you could get from a 10-year Treasury in mid-October. And while Treasury payouts are rock solid, Texas Instruments' profits can swing with the business cycle. The company could still deliver solid returns if it keeps growing earnings and raising the dividend, but the current price gives investors less cushion if things don't go as planned.
Looking at the competition, it's easy to see why a little caution is smart. Analog Devices, for example, traded at about 23.2 times forward earnings, well below Texas Instruments' 27.55. TXN's bigger scale and wide range of analog products might explain the higher price, but to keep that edge, the company will need to deliver more than just a return to normal demand. Sustained earnings growth is a must.
3. Dividend growth meets a demanding price
In September, TI announced it was bumping its quarterly dividend up by 7% to $1.52, or $6.08 per year. Based on the October 16 share price of $276.48, that's a forward yield of about 2.2%. The company's payout ratio sits at around 85%. A comparison with other established dividend payers, such as those featured in our unstoppable dividend stocks list, also puts TXN's modest 2.2% yield into perspective.
TI's 23-year track record of raising its dividend and its growing cash flow make it appealing for income-focused investors. But with a payout ratio this high, there's not much room for earnings to slip without putting the dividend at risk. Big spending on factories and the ups and downs of industry demand are still key risks, especially if the recovery loses steam.
Texas Instruments brings real long-term strengths and a steadily rising dividend to the table, but today's valuation means it can't afford to stumble. With a forward earnings yield lower than Treasuries and a high payout ratio, the case for buying in now relies mainly on the company's ability to keep growing its profits and raising its dividend.

Did The Market Read Texas Instruments Stock Right?
Tue, October 20, 2026 at 4:30 PM CDT 3 min read
Shares of Texas Instruments (TXN) rose 60.4% in the twelve months to October 19, 2026, against 16.8% for the S&P 500. The stock posted its largest one-day gain in that time on April 23, 2026. It climbed 19.4% the day after the chip maker reported first-quarter results and forecast second-quarter revenue above Wall Street estimates. So what changed inside Texas Instruments to earn that price?
Texas Instruments' Sales Growth Picked Up In 2026
Texas Instruments has issued four quarterly reports since last October. Sales growth slowed in the first two periods, from 16.4% in fiscal Q2 2025 to 14.2% in fiscal Q3 2025 and 10.4% in fiscal Q4 2025. Growth then picked up in the next two quarters. Revenue climbed 18.6% in fiscal Q1 2026, and rose 22.8% to $5.46 billion in fiscal Q2 2026.
Reuters tied both forecasts that came before the stock's biggest jumps to data centers. In January, the news agency linked a jump in the shares on January 28 to a first-quarter outlook that signaled robust AI data center demand. The stock closed 9.9% higher that day. In April, Reuters said Texas Instruments expected a boost in demand for its analog chips from data center development. On the fiscal Q2 2026 call in July, management said data center revenue had doubled from a year earlier.

Investors Paid Up Faster Than Texas Instruments' Profit Grew
Texas Instruments also kept more of those sales as profit. Over the twelve months to June 30, 2026, revenue grew 16.7%. The company earned an operating margin of 38.1% in that time, up from 34.9% a year earlier. Free cash flow over the same twelve months rose to $5.36 billion from $1.5 billion.
The share price rose faster than earnings, though. At the end of June 2026, the shares traded at 44.9 times trailing earnings, up from 37.4 a year earlier. That was the highest multiple at any quarter end since 2016, so the share price ran ahead of the earnings recovery. At the October 19, 2026 close, the multiple was 41.6, against 22.9 for the S&P 500.
What Has Not Changed At Texas Instruments
Texas Instruments has won back its sales, but it has not grown past its last peak. Revenue of $19.5 billion in the twelve months to June 2026 is about where it stood four years earlier, at $19.6 billion. In those earlier twelve months, the company kept far more of each dollar, with an operating margin of 52.7%, while its shares traded at 16.5 times earnings.
That gap in margin is what the business has not closed, even as the shares rose. Operating margin was 42.6% in fiscal Q2 2026, and it is the measure to watch when Texas Instruments next reports, expected on or around October 21, 2026.

Texas Instruments and Lam Research Report Earnings: AI Equipment Boom Meets Analog Rebound
Lam Research and Texas Instruments both report after the close on Wednesday, and each faces a different kind of pressure: one must prove AI equipment demand is still accelerating, while the other needs to show its industrial recovery has real…
Published October 20, 2026, 7:50am ET · 3 min read
Automated robotic arms meticulously assemble electronic components on an advanced manufacturing line, illustrating the high-tech production methods driving growth in the semiconductor industry, particularly for AI equipment and industrial applications. © Shutterstock
Two chip stocks from opposite ends of the industry report on Wednesday, October 21, after the market close. Lam Research (NASDAQ:LRCX | LRCX Price Prediction) has to show that AI equipment demand is still accelerating. Texas Instruments (NASDAQ:TXN) has to show that its industrial and auto rebound can last.
Texas Instruments hosts its call at 3:30 p.m. Central time (4:30 p.m. ET). Lam follows at 5:00 p.m. ET.
Texas Instruments Faces a Test of Its Own Guidance
Texas Instruments makes analog chips that handle real-world signals like power and temperature. It also makes embedded processors, the small control chips built into machines. On its prior earnings call, Texas Instruments said revenue rose 13% sequentially and 23% year over year. Industrial, data center, and automotive customers led the growth.
Texas Instruments guided third-quarter revenue to $5.65 billion to $6.15 billion and EPS to $2.23 to $2.57. The consensus EPS estimate of $2.42 falls inside that range, so the fourth-quarter outlook carries more weight. Management said industrial revenue remains below its 2022 peak and customer inventories have not been rebuilt. Auto demand picked up, led by electric vehicles and hybrids in China. Shares are up 59.2% year to date.
Lam Research Rides AI Demand Into Record Guidance
Lam sells deposition and etch tools, the machines that add and carve away thin layers of material on silicon wafers. On its prior earnings call, Lam said it delivered record revenue, operating margin, and earnings per share “as AI-driven demand continues to reshape the semiconductor industry,” positioning it for “a third consecutive year of outperformance in 2026.”
Lam guided September-quarter revenue to $8.1 billion, plus or minus $400 million, and EPS to $2.15 plus or minus $0.15. It also raised its 2026 forecast for wafer fab equipment spending (what the whole industry spends on chipmaking tools) to the low $150 billion range.
In an August 26 Bloomberg Businessweek report, Lam Research said its advanced packaging business is growing more than 70% year over year. Advanced packaging stacks memory and processor chips in three dimensions and wires them together, so AI hardware works like one large system. Lam shares are down 12.1% over the past week and up 59.0% year to date.
Consensus Points to Steep Year-Over-Year Gains
Jim Cramer described the demand picture on October 19, saying CPUs are “going to be in very short supply, which I think is absolutely true because Taiwan Semi can’t make all the ones that they have.” He added, “There’s tremendous demand, and there’s also an inability to build.” On October 9, he said, “Taiwan Semi controlled pretty much any chip stock.”
When chipmakers cannot build fast enough, they add factory capacity, and that means buying more deposition and etch tools from Lam. Lam said the industry remains meaningfully undersupplied, with several new fabs expected to come online by the end of 2027. The same buildout is pulling in power, cooling, and networking suppliers alongside the chipmakers. (We rounded up seven of those names in a free AI infrastructure report.)
What Each Company Must Prove on Wednesday
Texas Instruments needs a fourth-quarter outlook showing that industrial and automotive demand is still climbing. Lam needs revenue close to its $8.1 billion guidance and more detail on 2027, a year management already called a potentially strong setup.

What does the USD 360.00 target mean?
The latest reported quarter provides the operating benchmark. Texas Instruments posted USD 5.46 billion of revenue and USD 2.14 diluted earnings per share for the second quarter of 2026, with revenue up 22.8 percent year over year, according to EarningsMadness. The Zacks Analyst Blog Highlights Meta Platforms, Lam Research, Texas Instruments, Tesla, Netflix, Procter & Gamble and GE Aerospace
Tue, October 20, 2026 at 6:27 AM CDT 6 min read
Chicago, IL – October 20, 2026 – Zacks.com announces the list of stocks featured in the Analyst Blog. Every day the Zacks Equity Research analysts discuss the latest news and events impacting stocks and the financial markets. Stocks recently featured in the blog include: Meta Platforms META, Lam Research LRCX, Texas Instruments TXN, Tesla TSLA, Netflix NFLX, Procter & Gamble PG and GE Aerospace GE.
Here are highlights from Monday's Analyst Blog:
Q3 Earnings Reports Gear Up: Global Week Ahead
What happens across this Global Week Ahead?
· Q3 earnings season is shifting up a gear in the U.S., and
· Mainland China is about to deliver a deluge of macro data
· Giving febrile markets plenty more to ponder after the latest bouts of volatility in bonds and AI stocks
Elsewhere:
· Central bankers in Indonesia and Turkey have been given headaches by global index provider MSCI, while
· Voters in Brazil gear up to choose their next president
Next are Reuters' five world market themes, re-ordered for equity traders—
U.S. earnings season picks up in the coming days, with investors focused on Meta Platforms and other AI-focused companies as technology shares wobble.
Meta, due on Wednesday, is one of several hyper-scalers whose massive spending on AI data centers and infrastructure has been a big driver of investment.
With concerns mounting over financing for the AI buildout, investors want more detail on expected returns from those huge outlays.
Reports from semiconductor companies Lam Research and Texas Instruments will offer another view of the AI boom, as will results from Elon Musk's Tesla.
Other high-profile results in the coming days include Netflix, Procter & Gamble and GE Aerospace.
S&P500 earnings are expected to have climbed more than +30% in the third quarter, according to LSEG IBES, continuing a robust year for corporate profits.
(2) Stock & Bond Returns Correlation a Focus
For months, as energy and food prices surged amid the Iran war, bonds lost their shock-absorber status as investors jacked up estimates of how high interest rates might need to go.
Add near-chronic concern ‌about developed-world governments' finances, and bonds seemed to offer little safe-haven comfort while still struggling to rival super-charged equities.
The correlation between stocks and bond yields has now turned positive for Europe and the U.S., meaning yields are more likely to fall when stocks fall.
It had been overwhelmingly negative this year, with yields rising as stocks fell, undermining bonds' traditional role as a haven during equity selloffs.
This relationship fluctuates, but this year, the correlation of U.S. stocks and bond yields in March hit its most negative since at least the 1990s, while for European assets, it reached its most negative on record in September.
(3) MSCI Proposed Stripping Indonesia of EM Status. Turkey Put on Notice, Too
Central bankers in Indonesia and Turkey already have plenty on their plates.
Now they have an MSCI headache, too.
Indonesia's central bank meets on Wednesday, while Turkish policymakers gather on Thursday, against a backdrop of high energy prices, rising borrowing costs, AI-driven market disruption and geopolitical uncertainty.
MSCI has proposed stripping Indonesia of its emerging-market (EM) status and removing it from a suite of indexes, a move that risks triggering heavy outflows and raising pressure on policymakers to hike from 5.75% rather than hold.
MSCI has also put Turkey on notice, warning of a potential downgrade if market reforms fall short by mid-2027, another complication for policymakers expected to keep cutting rates from 37%.
(4) The Week Starts with a Mainland China Macro Data Deluge
A health check on the Chinese economy is due on Monday, with third-quarter GDP alongside September retail sales, industrial output and fixed-asset investment data.
The latest loan prime rate follows on Tuesday and is expected to stay put after more than a year on hold.
Strong global demand for semiconductors, clean technology and other manufactured goods has kept China's economy ticking, even as domestic demand remains patchy and higher energy costs bite.
Exports have held up despite China's delicate trade balancing act with the U.S. and E.U.
The latest trade figures showed Chinese exports surging well beyond analysts' estimates, putting the country on track for another $1 trillion trade surplus this year after crossing the threshold for the first time in 2025.
The flip side: the export boom could add to trade tensions with major partners.
(4) Brazil's Presidential Runoff Happens on October 25th. Campaigning Underway
Brazil's October 25th presidential runoff is keeping markets on edge after Flávio Bolsonaro's surprise first-round lead sent stocks up 7.7% and the real almost 4% higher.
A new Quaest poll puts Bolsonaro on 46% versus Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva's 44%, a technical tie.
Investors are betting a Bolsonaro win would bring tighter fiscal policy, but much may already be priced in. His choice of economic team and signs of credible reform could fuel further gains.
A Lula comeback, meanwhile, could put that rally into reverse, with the real, longer-dated bonds and state-controlled companies among the most exposed. A more conservative Congress, though, could limit how far Lula could shift policy.

Texas Instruments: 3 Things to Watch Before Buying the Dividend Stock
Mon, October 19, 2026 at 10:27 PM CDT 4 min read
Texas Instruments Incorporated (NASDAQ:TXN) stands out as a favorite among long-term dividend investors. The company's analog chips and embedded processors power everything from industrial machines and cars to data centers and home electronics. Because these products stick around for years, Texas Instruments enjoys steady repeat business and a real edge over competitors, thanks to its manufacturing know-how, engineering talent, and strong customer ties. These qualities also explain why the company often features in discussions of durable income-generating businesses, including Top 10 Unstoppable Dividend Stocks to Buy. Still, investors have to pay a premium for that kind of stability. Still, investors have to pay a premium for that kind of stability.
Texas Instruments' forward P/E is 27.55, while its trailing P/E sits much higher at 41.43. That gap shows investors expect earnings to bounce back from last year's lower numbers.
Find TXN among 10 Reliable Dividend Stocks to Buy for Long-Term Investors
Texas Instruments: 3 Things to Watch Before Buying the Dividend Stock
1. Earnings recovery is real, but not risk-free
The most recent quarter backs up the idea that things are turning around. In Q2 2026, revenue jumped 23% year over year to $5.46 billion, and net income surged 53% to $1.98 billion. Operating profit also climbed 48% to $2.31 billion, pushing operating margins to about 42.3%. Strong demand from factories, data centers, and automakers drove those gains.
Cash flow got a boost too. Over the past year, Texas Instruments Incorporated (NASDAQ:TXN) generated $6.53 billion in free cash flow, though that total includes $1.18 billion from CHIPS Act incentives. That's important because manufacturing investments, depreciation, and when government incentives hit the books all play a role in how much cash is left for dividends and buybacks.
2. Forward P/E: better than the past, but not a bargain
At a forward P/E of 27.55, TXN now trades higher than its forward multiples of 25.58 at the end of 2025 and 26.25 in September 2025, according to Yahoo Finance. The even higher trailing P/E of 41.43 highlights just how much last year's earnings were weighed down compared to what's expected going forward.
That forward P/E means investors are getting an earnings yield of just 3.63%, not great when you compare it to the 5.2% yield you could get from a 10-year Treasury in mid-October. And while Treasury payouts are rock solid, Texas Instruments' profits can swing with the business cycle. The company could still deliver solid returns if it keeps growing earnings and raising the dividend, but the current price gives investors less cushion if things don't go as planned.
Looking at the competition, it's easy to see why a little caution is smart. Analog Devices, for example, traded at about 23.2 times forward earnings, well below Texas Instruments' 27.55. TXN's bigger scale and wide range of analog products might explain the higher price, but to keep that edge, the company will need to deliver more than just a return to normal demand. Sustained earnings growth is a must.
3. Dividend growth meets a demanding price
In September, TI announced it was bumping its quarterly dividend up by 7% to $1.52, or $6.08 per year. Based on the October 16 share price of $276.48, that's a forward yield of about 2.2%. The company's payout ratio sits at around 85%. A comparison with other established dividend payers, such as those featured in our unstoppable dividend stocks list, also puts TXN's modest 2.2% yield into perspective.
TI's 23-year track record of raising its dividend and its growing cash flow make it appealing for income-focused investors. But with a payout ratio this high, there's not much room for earnings to slip without putting the dividend at risk. Big spending on factories and the ups and downs of industry demand are still key risks, especially if the recovery loses steam.
Texas Instruments brings real long-term strengths and a steadily rising dividend to the table, but today's valuation means it can't afford to stumble. With a forward earnings yield lower than Treasuries and a high payout ratio, the case for buying in now relies mainly on the company's ability to keep growing its profits and raising its dividend.
While we acknowledge the risk and potential of TXN as an investment, our conviction lies in the belief that some AI stocks hold greater promise for delivering higher returns and doing so within a shorter time frame. The useful question is how much that cash can decline before the advantage disappears, rather than assuming today's memory economics last a decade. Sandisk vs. Texas Instruments: How Much Cash-Yield Protection Does Memory Offer?
Reconcile the cash before comparing the price
Sandisk's fiscal 2026 operating cash was $11.671 billion. Deduct $177 million of direct capital spending and $275 million of net manufacturing-joint-venture funding, and $11.219 billion remains. Removing a further $2.591 billion increase in refund and contract liabilities leaves $8.628 billion for this diagnostic comparison.
That last adjustment tests cash supported by customer funding. It is not a full estimate of normal earnings, and it differs from the company's $8.743 billion adjusted free-cash-flow measure because the liability adjustment is broader. Other working-capital and tax effects remain.
Texas Instruments generated $8.667 billion of operating cash over the twelve months through June. Deducting $3.312 billion of capital spending leaves $5.355 billion before separate capital-incentive proceeds. Operating cash still includes $433 million of investment-tax-credit benefits, so this is not a fully subsidy-free measure.
Against October 16 equity values of $190.24 billion and $252.49 billion, the resulting cash yields are 4.5% for Sandisk and 2.1% for Texas Instruments. Sandisk's adjusted residual could fall about 53% before matching Texas Instruments' current yield, if prices and the latter's cash stayed fixed.
That is a break-even calculation, not a downside limit. With a 60% decline in Sandisk's residual, its yield would fall to about 1.8%, below the analog company's starting yield. Our Sandisk business analysis examines the demand and pricing conditions behind today's profits.
Texas Instruments offers long-lived products and broader applications, but its factories also need utilization. New capacity can depress cash returns before demand catches up, and a large dividend leaves less room to retain cash. Sandisk's joint ventures share manufacturing investment while preserving fixed-cost and funding obligations. Sandisk's August investor day supplied a counterargument: eight customer agreements carry committed volumes, minimum financial guarantees and structured pricing. Management expects them to cover about half of fiscal 2027 bits. Those contracts may reduce old-cycle volatility, although their performance through a downturn remains unproven.

A dividend is not an independent source of protection.

As a simple stress test, cut each company's operating cash by 20%, hold capital spending and historical dividends fixed, and coverage falls to 0.71 times for Texas Instruments versus 2.73 for Broadcom.

Did The Market Read Texas Instruments Stock Right?
Tue, October 20, 2026 at 4:30 PM CDT 3 min read
Shares of Texas Instruments (TXN) rose 60.4% in the twelve months to October 19, 2026, against 16.8% for the S&P 500. The stock posted its largest one-day gain in that time on April 23, 2026. It climbed 19.4% the day after the chip maker reported first-quarter results and forecast second-quarter revenue above Wall Street estimates. So what changed inside Texas Instruments to earn that price?
Texas Instruments' Sales Growth Picked Up In 2026
Texas Instruments has issued four quarterly reports since last October. Sales growth slowed in the first two periods, from 16.4% in fiscal Q2 2025 to 14.2% in fiscal Q3 2025 and 10.4% in fiscal Q4 2025. Growth then picked up in the next two quarters. Revenue climbed 18.6% in fiscal Q1 2026, and rose 22.8% to $5.46 billion in fiscal Q2 2026.
Reuters tied both forecasts that came before the stock's biggest jumps to data centers. In January, the news agency linked a jump in the shares on January 28 to a first-quarter outlook that signaled robust AI data center demand. The stock closed 9.9% higher that day. In April, Reuters said Texas Instruments expected a boost in demand for its analog chips from data center development. On the fiscal Q2 2026 call in July, management said data center revenue had doubled from a year earlier.

Investors Paid Up Faster Than Texas Instruments' Profit Grew
Texas Instruments also kept more of those sales as profit. Over the twelve months to June 30, 2026, revenue grew 16.7%. The company earned an operating margin of 38.1% in that time, up from 34.9% a year earlier. Free cash flow over the same twelve months rose to $5.36 billion from $1.5 billion.
The share price rose faster than earnings, though. At the end of June 2026, the shares traded at 44.9 times trailing earnings, up from 37.4 a year earlier. That was the highest multiple at any quarter end since 2016, so the share price ran ahead of the earnings recovery. At the October 19, 2026 close, the multiple was 41.6, against 22.9 for the S&P 500.
What Has Not Changed At Texas Instruments
Texas Instruments has won back its sales, but it has not grown past its last peak. Revenue of $19.5 billion in the twelve months to June 2026 is about where it stood four years earlier, at $19.6 billion. In those earlier twelve months, the company kept far more of each dollar, with an operating margin of 52.7%, while its shares traded at 16.5 times earnings.
That gap in margin is what the business has not closed, even as the shares rose. Operating margin was 42.6% in fiscal Q2 2026, and it is the measure to watch when Texas Instruments next reports, expected on or around October 21, 2026.

Conference call at 3:30 p.m. Central time today on ti.com/ir
DALLAS (July 22, 2026) – Texas Instruments Incorporated (TI) (Nasdaq: TXN) today reported second quarter revenue of $5.46 billion, net income of $1.98 billion and earnings per share of $2.14. Earnings per share included a 5-cent benefit that was not in the company's original guidance.
Regarding the company's performance and returns to shareholders, Haviv Ilan, TI's chairman, president and CEO, made the following comments:
•"Revenue increased 13% sequentially and 23% from the same quarter a year ago with broad growth led by industrial, data center and automotive.
•"Our cash flow from operations of $8.7 billion for the trailing 12 months again underscored the strength of our business model, the quality of our product portfolio and the benefit of 300mm production. Free cash flow for the same period was $6.5 billion.
•"Over the past 12 months we invested $3.9 billion in R&D and SG&A, invested $3.3 billion in capital expenditures and returned $5.8 billion to owners.
•"TI's third quarter outlook is for revenue in the range of $5.65 billion to $6.15 billion and earnings per share between $2.23 and $2.57."
Free cash flow, a non-GAAP financial measure, is cash flow from operations less capital expenditures, plus proceeds from U.S. CHIPS and Science Act (CHIPS Act) incentives.

Free cash flow is calculated as cash flows from operating activities (also referred to as cash flow from operations) less capital expenditures, plus proceeds from CHIPS Act incentives.
We believe that free cash flow and the associated ratios provide insight into our liquidity, our cash-generating capability and the amount of cash potentially available to return to shareholders, as well as insight into our financial performance. This release includes forward-looking statements intended to qualify for the safe harbor from liability established by the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995. These forward-looking statements generally can be identified by phrases such as TI or its management "believes," "expects," "anticipates," "foresees," "forecasts," "estimates" or other words or phrases of similar import. Similarly, statements herein that describe TI's business strategy, outlook, objectives, plans, intentions or goals also are forward-looking statements. All such forward-looking statements are subject to certain risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially from those in forward-looking statements.
We urge you to carefully consider the following important factors that could cause actual results to differ materially from the expectations of TI or our management:
•Economic, social and political conditions, and natural events in the countries in which we, our customers or our suppliers operate, including global trade policies;
•Our ability to compete in products and prices in an intensely competitive industry;
•Market demand for semiconductors, particularly in the industrial and automotive markets, and customer demand that differs from forecasts;
•Losses or curtailments of purchases from key customers or the timing and amount of customer inventory adjustments;
•Evolving cybersecurity and other threats relating to our information technology systems or those of our customers, suppliers and other third parties;
•Our ability to successfully implement and realize opportunities from strategic, business and organizational changes, or our ability to realize our expectations regarding the amount and timing of associated restructuring charges and cost savings;
•Our ability to develop, manufacture and market innovative products in a rapidly changing technological environment, our timely implementation of new manufacturing technologies and installation of manufacturing equipment, and our ability to realize expected returns on significant investments in manufacturing capacity;
•Availability and cost of key materials, utilities, manufacturing equipment, third-party manufacturing services and manufacturing technology;
•Our ability to retain, train and recruit skilled personnel and effectively manage key employee succession;
•Product liability, warranty or other claims relating to our products, software, manufacturing, delivery, services, design or communications, or recalls by our customers for a product containing one of our parts;
•Financial difficulties of our distributors or semiconductor distributors' promotion of competing product lines to our detriment; or disputes with current or former distributors;
•Our ability to maintain or improve profit margins, including our ability to utilize our manufacturing facilities at sufficient levels to cover our fixed operating costs, in an intensely competitive and cyclical industry and changing regulatory environment;
•Compliance with or changes in the complex laws, rules and regulations to which we are or may become subject, or actions of enforcement authorities, that restrict our ability to operate our business or subject us to fines, penalties or other legal liability;
•Changes in tax law and accounting standards that impact the tax rate applicable to us, the jurisdictions in which profits are determined to be earned and taxed, adverse resolution of tax audits, increases in tariff rates, and the ability to realize deferred tax assets;
•Our ability to maintain and enforce a strong intellectual property portfolio and maintain freedom of operation in all jurisdictions where we conduct business; or our exposure to infringement claims;
•Our ability to make principal and interest payments on our debt when due;
•Instability in the global credit and financial markets; and
•Impairments of our non-financial assets.
For a more detailed discussion of these factors, see the Risk factors discussion in Item 1A of TI's most recent Form 10-K. The forward-looking statements included in this release are made only as of the date of this release, and we undertake no obligation to update the forward-looking statements to reflect subsequent events or circumstances. If we do update any forward-looking statement, you should not infer that we will make additional updates with respect to that statement or any other forward-looking statement.
Texas Instruments Incorporated (Nasdaq: TXN) is a global semiconductor company that designs, manufactures and sells analog and embedded processing chips for markets such as industrial, automotive, data center, personal electronics and communications equipment. At our core, we have a passion to create a better world by making electronics more affordable through semiconductors. This passion is alive today as each generation of innovation builds upon the last to make our technology more reliable, more affordable and lower power, making it possible for semiconductors to go into electronics everywhere. Learn more at TI.com.

The stock closed at $227.39 on October 16. It has returned 110.0% over the last 6 months, compared with a 10.5% return for the Insider Monkey Billionaire Index and 9.3% for the State Street SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust.
A fall that size usually takes some of the risk out of a share price. Whether it did here depends on how much was in there to begin with.

What the Business Is Doing:
Revenue rose 25.80% in the three months just gone, and the business generated $1.61 billion of operating cash flow in its last financial year.
What sits behind that is one piece of software already running on the customer’s machines. CrowdStrike sells further modules onto that same sensor, so a customer buying its next product installs nothing new. Selling more into an existing account costs little more than switching it on.
That is also why the accounts stay. Replacing the system that watches for intrusions means running two during the handover, or none at all, and a security team does not volunteer for either. Security is usually among the last budget lines a company trims.
The balance sheet puts no pressure on any of it. Borrowings are small against equity, and the business covers its own spending from cash, so a weak year would not force a decision.

What the Price Still Assumes:
The shares cost 208.33 times what analysts expect next year. A multiple in that range does not price a good business. It prices one that cannot disappoint for several years running.
The reported figures leave little underneath it. The operating margin is still negative at -2.26%, so the company does not yet make money on its sales as it reports them, and the earnings the multiple is measured against are adjusted ones. What sits between the two is mostly stock handed to staff, a cost that never leaves as cash but still counts against reported profit.
The run into that price is the context. The fall came after a steep climb earlier in the year, so one bad session has barely dented what came before.

What the Selloff Changed:
Very little. A fall of that size takes a multiple this large down by a few points and leaves it in the same category it was in the day before.
The question a buyer faces also remains unchanged. Growth has to stay in the mid-twenties for years, and the margin has to turn, because the price has already counted both.
A high multiple needs everything to go right. 10 Most Profitable Undervalued Stocks to Invest In looks where less has to.
Conclusion:
The selloff did not make this cheap and was never likely to. What CrowdStrike has is a growing business paid for out of a defended budget, funded without meaningful debt, and that is the reason anyone owns it. What the price asks for is years of the same without a stumble, measured against earnings that are adjusted rather than reported. Watch whether the reported margin turns positive, because until it does, the valuation rests entirely on the adjusted version.

The Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ) is up 0.6%, so the strength is concentrated in security software while large-cap tech posts a modest advance.
Accelerator Puts Falcon at the Center of Agentic Security
CrowdStrike announced the fourth annual edition of its Cybersecurity Startup Accelerator, aimed at early-stage companies building protection products for the agentic era. That term describes software agents that act on their own without waiting for a human instruction, and participants in the CrowdStrike program get an accelerated path to build on its platform, including access to Falcon Foundry agent-creation tools and the company’s programming interfaces.
Startups in the CrowdStrike accelerator can also develop verified integrations and publish in the CrowdStrike Marketplace, while Amazon Web Services adds partner onboarding and marketplace listing support. NVIDIA provides technical training through its startup program. Across its editions, the accelerator has backed more than ninety startups, several since acquired, including one bought by CrowdStrike itself.
The accelerator works as a platform move for CrowdStrike, since it recruits outside companies to build on Falcon and turns access to the CrowdStrike ecosystem into the offering. Daniel Bernard is chief business officer at CrowdStrike. He stated that the next generation of agentic cybersecurity companies is being built now and that the three partners are putting their scale behind those founders. Bernard added that when those companies expand, CrowdStrike grows with them.
Year to date, CrowdStrike stock is up 140%, and that run is the figure to measure against the enthusiasm. An ecosystem announcement doesn’t carry revenue with it, so the return for CrowdStrike from the accelerator sits further out. Follow-through in CrowdStrike’s reported results would do more to justify that climb than any partnership headline.
The next test for CrowdStrike is whether its agentic positioning turns into modules customers pay for, since partnerships that generate goodwill and little else would leave CrowdStrike stock leaning on sentiment. Investors will want to see signs that accelerator startups ship verified integrations and that those connections pull added Falcon modules into existing CrowdStrike accounts.
With Palo Alto and Zscaler shares posting the bigger moves, the breadth of the sector is the cleaner read on demand for AI security. Traders may want to keep an eye on whether the cybersecurity group holds its gains into the close relative to the Invesco QQQ Trust. CrowdStrike (CRWD -0.32%) and Docusign (DOCU +4.72%) represent two distinct paths within the software market, as one pursues aggressive expansion in cybersecurity while the other refocuses on broader agreement lifecycles.
CrowdStrike is a leader in endpoint security, whereas Docusign dominates the electronic signature market. Investors often compare them to determine whether the premium price of a security leader outweighs the value proposition of a workflow giant.
CrowdStrike provides AI-native cybersecurity through its Falcon platform, which secures endpoints, identities, and data for enterprises and governments. The company relies on Amazon (AMZN +0.07%) as a key third-party data center provider to deliver its cloud-based services. In its latest annual report, the company noted that it has focused on rebuilding customer trust following a major content configuration incident in mid-2024 while expanding into tech stocks related to artificial intelligence initiatives.
In FY 2026, revenue reached nearly $4.8 billion, representing growth of approximately 21.7% over the previous year. Despite this top-line expansion, the company reported a net loss of roughly $162.5 million for the period. This resulted in a net margin of -3.4%, reflecting a shift from the nominal net loss in the prior fiscal year as the company continues to invest in platform scale.
As of its January 2026 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is approximately 0.2x. This ratio measures total debt relative to the value provided by shareholders. The current ratio, which measures a company's ability to cover its short-term bills with its short-term assets, is close to 1.8x. Free cash flow reached nearly $1.3 billion, though stock-based compensation accounted for roughly 68% of operating cash flow, inflating reported cash generation because SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.
Docusign has shifted its focus toward the Intelligent Agreement Management (IAM) platform, which helps organizations manage the entire lifecycle of a contract. The company serves over 1.8 million customers and maintains strategic partnerships with leaders like Salesforce (CRM -0.01%), Microsoft (MSFT -0.31%), SAP (SAP +1.30%), ServiceNow (NOW +2.88%), and Workday (WDAY +4.50%). It also integrates with platforms owned by Alphabet to ensure its tools are accessible within standard office workflows.
In FY 2026, revenue reached approximately $3.2 billion, an increase of about 8.2% from the prior year. The company reported net income of roughly $309.1 million, resulting in a net margin of approximately 9.6%. Although this net margin is lower than in the previous fiscal year, the company remains consistently profitable as it transitions users to its new IAM products.
As of its January 2026 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio reached nearly 0.1x. The current ratio is approximately 0.7x, indicating that the company has fewer short-term assets than short-term liabilities. Free cash flow was close to $1.1 billion for the fiscal year. Note that stock-based compensation represented roughly 53.4% of operating cash flow, which inflates reported cash generation since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.
CrowdStrike faces significant risks regarding operational and reputational damage following its July 2024 system incident, which led to increased litigation and potential customer churn. The company also operates in an intense competitive landscape where legacy vendors and new AI entrants exert pricing pressure. Furthermore, its reliance on third-party cloud infrastructure and the evolving global data privacy landscape, such as the EU AI Act, could impose higher compliance costs and operational constraints.
Docusign faces high dependency on its eSignature product for the majority of its subscription revenue, which makes it vulnerable if market adoption slows. Rapid advancements in AI technology could allow competitors or customers to build internal alternatives, potentially disrupting its business model. The company also faces competition from Adobe and must navigate complex international regulations, including GDPR, that impact its global data management and security operations.
Docusign currently trades at a significant discount to CrowdStrike on both earnings and sales metrics, reflecting its slower growth profile compared to the cybersecurity leader.

Cybersecurity has become an essential service for businesses of all sizes, and CrowdStrike's Falcon platform continues to attract customers and generate revenue: $4.81 billion in FY 2026, up nearly 22% year over year. Fortinet, Inc. (NASDAQ:FTNT) and CrowdStrike Holdings, Inc. (NASDAQ:CRWD) each reported roughly 26% revenue growth in their latest quarters. Investors nevertheless pay about 53 times Fortinet’s current-year adjusted earnings guidance and 215 times CrowdStrike’s. The gap raises a useful question: how much more should durable subscription growth cost when the cheaper company already earns substantial reported profits?
The multiples use October 2 closing prices of $180.95 and $270.04, divided by guidance midpoints of $3.44 and $1.255. Fortinet’s year ends December 2026; CrowdStrike’s ends January 2027. CrowdStrike’s price and earnings are both adjusted for July’s four-for-one split. Our earlier CrowdStrike–Palo Alto valuation comparison tests a different rival; Fortinet adds a sharper hardware-versus-subscription challenge.
The same growth rate hides different engines
Fortinet’s June-quarter product revenue jumped 52%, while services grew 14%. Hardware demand can arrive in bursts as customers upgrade networks.Converting the product surge into recurring service revenue would make growth more durable when the hardware upgrade cycle slows. That matters when judging the businesses in our high-growth, low-debt stock screen: financial flexibility and growth durability answer different questions.
CrowdStrike’s July-quarter ending annual recurring revenue grew 25% to $5.84 billion. Net new ARR increased 51% to $333 million, supporting a case for accelerating customer commitments. Its security platform spans endpoints, identity and cloud workloads. Our agentic-AI stock shortlist examines where security fits among the platforms companies need as automated work spreads.
Fortinet is also expanding beyond appliances. Management reported 35% billings growth in Unified SASE, which combines networking and security services, and 25% in AI-driven Security Operations. These are billings measures, not recognized revenue. The premium requires more durable, profitable growth. Our analysis of cybersecurity’s split from the AI infrastructure trade asks why security budgets might follow a different spending cycle.
Insider Monkey’s Q2 2026 holder count rose to 62 from 52 in Q1 for Fortinet and to 89 from 79 for CrowdStrike. Arrowstreet increased Fortinet shares about 5%; D. E. Shaw increased CrowdStrike shares 18%. The competing business models both drew broader fund ownership.
Reported profits change the burden of proof
Fortinet earned a 33.7% GAAP operating margin in Q2. CrowdStrike recorded a $33.2 million GAAP operating loss on $1.47 billion of revenue, despite substantial adjusted profit. CrowdStrike’s reconciliation adds back $399 million of stock compensation and related payroll taxes, about 27% of revenue. That makes a fourfold adjusted-earnings multiple gap especially demanding.
Cash flow provides a second lens. Fortinet generated reported $966 million of free cash flow, or 47.2% of revenue, while CrowdStrike reported $377 million, or about 26%; their free-cash-flow definitions differ. Collections and working capital make one quarter an imperfect comparison, and stock compensation can support cash flow while diluting shareholders. Our cash-flow screen that includes Fortinet examines that distinction; our return-on-equity ranking shows why high reported profitability also needs a balance-sheet check.
CrowdStrike’s strongest defense is a longer growth runway. Security agents could increase the value of its installed platform and proprietary customer context. The commercial question behind its cybersecurity work with Nvidia is whether that advantage becomes incremental revenue. Its expanded OpenAI partnership presents a related test: better models must strengthen pricing power enough to offset competition and deployment costs.
How much execution does the premium require?
As an illustration, if Fortinet’s adjusted earnings per share grew 15% annually for five years with both share prices unchanged, CrowdStrike would need roughly 52% annual earnings-per-share growth to reach Fortinet’s resulting multiple of about 26 times earnings. This is a valuation sensitivity, not a forecast; faster Fortinet growth would raise the hurdle. CrowdStrike can outperform without fully closing the gap, but continued premium pricing carries risk.
CrowdStrike’s September 15 short interest was 27.93 million shares, approximately 2.8% of float, with 2.42 days to cover. That dated snapshot offers limited support for a squeeze thesis.
Fortinet is my relative preference, though 53 times guided earnings still requires sustained growth. I would reconsider if its service growth stalls while CrowdStrike converts rising ARR into much faster per-share profits with less dilution. The risk explored in our analysis of AI and cybersecurity moats matters to both: stronger tools can expand demand while narrowing product differences. CrowdStrike must monetize that change exceptionally well to justify today’s price.

Is CrowdStrike (CRWD) Still Priced for Perfection After the October Selloff?
Tue, October 20, 2026 at 9:44 AM CDT 4 min read
CrowdStrike Holdings, Inc. (NASDAQ:CRWD) had a hard session on October 16, falling 7% while the wider market gave up a fraction of that.
The stock closed at $227.39 on October 16. It has returned 110.0% over the last 6 months, compared with a 10.5% return for the Insider Monkey Billionaire Index and 9.3% for the State Street SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust.
A fall that size usually takes some of the risk out of a share price. Whether it did here depends on how much was in there to begin with.

What the Business Is Doing:
Revenue rose 25.80% in the three months just gone, and the business generated $1.61 billion of operating cash flow in its last financial year.
What sits behind that is one piece of software already running on the customer's machines. CrowdStrike sells further modules onto that same sensor, so a customer buying its next product installs nothing new. Selling more into an existing account costs little more than switching it on.
That is also why the accounts stay. Replacing the system that watches for intrusions means running two during the handover, or none at all, and a security team does not volunteer for either. Security is usually among the last budget lines a company trims.
The balance sheet puts no pressure on any of it. Borrowings are small against equity, and the business covers its own spending from cash, so a weak year would not force a decision.

What the Price Still Assumes:
The shares cost 208.33 times what analysts expect next year. A multiple in that range does not price a good business. It prices one that cannot disappoint for several years running.
The reported figures leave little underneath it. The operating margin is still negative at -2.26%, so the company does not yet make money on its sales as it reports them, and the earnings the multiple is measured against are adjusted ones. What sits between the two is mostly stock handed to staff, a cost that never leaves as cash but still counts against reported profit.
The run into that price is the context. The fall came after a steep climb earlier in the year, so one bad session has barely dented what came before.

What the Selloff Changed:
Very little. A fall of that size takes a multiple this large down by a few points and leaves it in the same category it was in the day before.
The question a buyer faces also remains unchanged. Growth has to stay in the mid-twenties for years, and the margin has to turn, because the price has already counted both.
A high multiple needs everything to go right. 10 Most Profitable Undervalued Stocks to Invest In looks where less has to.
Conclusion:
The selloff did not make this cheap and was never likely to. What CrowdStrike has is a growing business paid for out of a defended budget, funded without meaningful debt, and that is the reason anyone owns it. What the price asks for is years of the same without a stumble, measured against earnings that are adjusted rather than reported. Watch whether the reported margin turns positive, because until it does, the valuation rests entirely on the adjusted version.

CrowdStrike Holdings, Inc. (NASDAQ:CRWD) was held by 89 hedge funds with a combined stake value of about $4.54 billion at the end of Q2 2026 in the Insider Monkey database. This is up from 79 hedge fund holders in the previous quarter.
