Wall Street Analysts See a 27.86% Upside in KLA (KLAC): Can the Stock Really Move This High?
Wed, October 14, 2026 at 7:55 AM CDT 4 min read
Shares of KLA (KLAC) have gained 9.5% over the past four weeks to close the last trading session at $184, but there could still be a solid upside left in the stock if short-term price targets of Wall Street analysts are any indication. Going by the price targets, the mean estimate of $235.26 indicates a potential upside of 27.9%.
The mean estimate comprises 27 short-term price targets with a standard deviation of $38.15. While the lowest estimate of $170.00 indicates a 7.6% decline from the current price level, the most optimistic analyst expects the stock to surge 76.6% to reach $325.00. It's very important to note the standard deviation here, as it helps understand the variability of the estimates. The smaller the standard deviation, the greater the agreement among analysts.
While the consensus price target is highly sought after by investors, the ability and unbiasedness of analysts in setting price targets have long been questionable. And investors making investment decisions solely based on this tool would arguably do themselves a disservice.
However, an impressive consensus price target is not the only factor that indicates a potential upside in KLAC. This view is strengthened by the agreement among analysts that the company will report better earnings than what they estimated earlier. Though a positive trend in earnings estimate revisions doesn't give any idea as to how much the stock could surge, it has proven effective in predicting an upside.
Zacks Price, Consensus and EPS Surprise Chart for KLAC
Here's What You May Not Know About Analysts' Price Targets
According to researchers at several universities across the globe, a price target is one of many pieces of information about a stock that misleads investors far more often than it guides. In fact, empirical research shows that price targets set by several analysts, irrespective of the extent of agreement, rarely indicate where the price of a stock could actually be heading.
While Wall Street analysts have deep knowledge of a company's fundamentals and the sensitivity of its business to economic and industry issues, many of them tend to set overly optimistic price targets. Are you wondering why?
They usually do that to drum up interest in shares of companies that their firms either have existing business relationships with or are looking to be associated with. In other words, business incentives of firms covering a stock often result in inflated price targets set by analysts.
However, a tight clustering of price targets, which is represented by a low standard deviation, indicates that analysts have a high degree of agreement about the direction and magnitude of a stock's price movement. While that doesn't necessarily mean the stock will hit the average price target, it could be a good starting point for further research aimed at identifying the potential fundamental driving forces.
That said, while investors should not entirely ignore price targets, making an investment decision solely based on them could lead to disappointing ROI. So, price targets should always be treated with a high degree of skepticism.
Analysts' growing optimism over the company's earnings prospects, as indicated by strong agreement among them in revising EPS estimates higher, could be a legitimate reason to expect an upside in the stock. That's because empirical research shows a strong correlation between trends in earnings estimate revisions and near-term stock price movements.
The Zacks Consensus Estimate for the current year has increased 0.4% over the past month, as one estimate has gone higher compared to no negative revision.
Moreover, KLAC currently has a Zacks Rank #2 (Buy), which means it is in the top 20% of more than 4,000 stocks that we rank based on four factors related to earnings estimates. Given an impressive externally-audited track record, this is a more conclusive indication of the stock's potential upside in the near term. Therefore, while the consensus price target may not be a reliable indicator of how much KLAC could gain, the direction of price movement it implies does appear to be a good guide.

One Reason KLA Stock Looks Better Than Its Price
Most investors still view KLA (KLAC) as a traditional wafer inspection company. However, the business selling inspection tools for advanced packaging is beginning to stand out, and management ties this demand to the expansion of AI. Packaging may be part of what buyers are currently paying for. The stock costs 51.4 times earnings, against 21.9 for the S&P 500, yet overall sales grew 15% from a year earlier in fiscal Q4 2026. A price that high beside that growth rate presents a clear contradiction. So, how big has KLA's packaging business become?
KLA's Packaging Forecast: About $1.1 Billion In Calendar 2026
Management expects about $1.1 billion of revenue from packaging process control systems in calendar 2026. That figure represents an increase of more than 70% from a year earlier. The company provided this raised forecast during its fiscal Q4 2026 call on July 28, 2026, stepping up from an earlier expectation of growth in the high 50% range.
Management stated that the expansion of AI requires new, complex packaging steps, alongside additional KLA systems to bring those processes to high-volume production. Furthermore, customers adopting newer packaging methods such as hybrid bonding are buying more inspection tools, the company said.
Packaging remains a small fraction of the overall business at KLA, which recorded $13.6 billion in sales over the last twelve months. Yet management expects this segment to grow more than 70% in calendar 2026.
Does Packaging Help KLA With Rising Costs?
Not directly. While packaging brings KLA more sales, the segment does not alter what the company pays for parts.
Costs surfaced repeatedly on the July 28 call. KLA is buying memory components at higher prices, and management indicated those headwinds will "likely continue through next year." When asked why the company could not simply raise its own prices to match, executives explained that it is difficult to adjust pricing on existing orders. Instead, new prices are established when new products come out.
Despite these material costs, gross margin reached 62.4% in fiscal Q4 2026, landing at the upper end of KLA's guidance. Looking ahead to the September quarter, which KLA has yet to report, management forecast 62.5%, plus or minus 1 percentage point.
Sales are also expanding. Management listed advanced packaging among the factors behind its record fiscal Q4 revenue of $3.66 billion. The company then guided to $4 billion for the September quarter, plus or minus $200 million.
Can KLA Build Its Tools Fast Enough?
Not during the first half of calendar 2026. Management noted that shortages of some long-lead-time materials held the company back during that period. KLA's lead times currently sit at about 12 months across the company, stretching closer to 18 to 24 months on certain products. Building new capacity for those components can take 12 to 24 months. KLA says it is adding capacity to support the demand it expects.
That timeline matters for the packaging business because the cited revenue figure is a forecast for the year, not a recorded result. KLA must physically build the tools before it can sell them.
Ultimately, KLA's packaging revenue forecast for calendar 2026 is the number to watch when the company reports its September quarter.

Now you know KLAC better. And that's our purpose: to make you informed before you invest your money. However, making a bet on a single stock carries its own risks.

If You Invested $1000 in KLA a Decade Ago, This is How Much It'd Be Worth Now
How much a stock's price changes over time is important for most investors, since price performance can both impact your investment portfolio and help you compare investment results across sectors and industries.
FOMO, or the fear of missing out, also plays a role in investing, particularly with tech giants and popular consumer-facing stocks.
What if you'd invested in KLA (KLAC) ten years ago? It may not have been easy to hold on to KLAC for all that time, but if you did, how much would your investment be worth today?
With that in mind, let's take a look at KLA's main business drivers.
Milpitas, CA-based KLA Corporation is an original equipment manufacturer (OEM) of process diagnostics and control (PDC) equipment and yield management solutions required for the fabrication of semiconductor integrated circuits (ICs) or chips. The company has a comprehensive portfolio of products addressing each major PDC subsegment, including photomask or reticle inspection, wafer inspection and defect review, and metrology.
Reticle production is vital to the semiconductor device formation process. Reticles control the precise deposition of materials onto the wafer, which changes its chemical characteristics and imparts specific functions to the ICs created. Inspection and metrology tools measure reticle quality and help improve production yields. The broader use of semiconductors, shrinking form factors and greater chip functionality continue to increase the importance of reticle design and production. Taiwan Semiconductor was the only largest customers in the last three years, accounting for more than 10% of total sales in fiscal 2026, 2025 and 2024.
KLA reported revenues of $13.58 billion in fiscal 2026. Product revenues accounted for 77% of total revenues, while service revenues represented 23%. Semiconductor Process Control generated $12.24 billion, or 90% of fiscal 2026 revenues. Specialty Semiconductor Process and PCB and Component Inspection contributed $584 million (4.3% of revenues) and $750 million (5.5% of reveneus), respectively.
KLA's two main product lines are defect inspection and metrology. Its defect inspection tools have broad applications in chip, wafer, reticle, storage, compound semiconductor and MEMS manufacturing. Metrology tools gather critical dimension measurements and assess process dimensions such as film thickness, lithography overlay and surface profiling. These products are used in chip, wafer, reticle and solar device manufacturing. KLA also offers products and services.
In addition to new tools, KLA offers refurbished systems that upgrade equipment and improve yields under the KT-Certified program. These tools are sold to IC, reticle, substrate, MEMS and data storage manufacturers.
Although KLA is a major player in each of its served markets, it faces competition from other large equipment suppliers such as Applied Materials and Hitachi High-Tech Corporation.
Putting together a successful investment portfolio takes a combination of research, patience, and a little bit of risk. For KLA, if you bought shares a decade ago, you're likely feeling really good about your investment today.
A $1000 investment made in October 2016 would be worth $27,085.45, or a gain of 2,608.55%, as of October 8, 2026, according to our calculations. This return excludes dividends but includes price appreciation.
In comparison, the S&P 500's gained 262.24% and the price of gold went up 211.21% over the same time frame.
Analysts are forecasting more upside for KLAC too.
KLA remains positioned to outperform as AI infrastructure spending broadens demand for process control across leading-edge logic, memory and advanced packaging. Rising chip complexity, larger die sizes and tighter defect requirements should increase inspection and metrology intensity. A backlog above $12 billion and improving supply availability provide visibility into 2027, while advanced packaging offers added share gains as front-end tools move into packaging flows. Services add recurring revenue as the installed base expands. KLA's differentiated portfolio, operating leverage and capital-return framework support long-term earnings growth. Risks include semiconductor cyclicality, customer concentration, export controls, competition and component costs, but structural demand and share opportunities remain more compelling.
The stock has jumped 7.61% over the past four weeks. Additionally, no earnings estimate has gone lower in the past two months, compared to 1 higher, for fiscal 2026; the consensus estimate has moved up as well.

Qualcomm is reportedly planning to lay off some of its employees globally. According to a Reuters report, the job cuts are part of a "performance-focused reduction" following the annual employee reviews. Qualcomm CEO Cristiano Amon has sent a memo to the staff, informing them of ‌notifications beginning in November. "We must have the right ​people in the right roles so they can perform at their best and the company can continue ​to succeed."
Qualcomm is one of the world's biggest smartphone chipmakers.
It has been hit this year by a slump in consumer electronics sales as rising memory prices impacted demand in key markets. The company’s shares have risen just 1.5% in 2026, compared with gains of more than ​12% for the benchmark S&P 500 and nearly 60% for the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index.Qualcomm released its latest earnings report earlier this year in July. The company then forecasted quarterly profit below estimates and said revenue from Apple products would decline faster than expected. However, it then signalled that growth in data-center and ​other non-handset businesses would ​more than offset ⁠the lost revenue by fiscal 2027. The company expects most of its chip sales to come from industries outside smartphones in fiscal 2027 as it expands into the fast-growing AI data centre market.

Qualcomm Pushes Back on Snapdragon Overheating Reports Tied to Galaxy S27 Ultra
Qualcomm rejects Snapdragon overheating claims amid reports of Samsung testing problems, raising questions about the Galaxy S27 Ultra’s processor.
Qualcomm has rejected overheating allegations involving its Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 processor as questions persist about Samsung's Galaxy S27 Ultra chip choice. Image: Qualcomm Technologies, Inc.

Qualcomm is rejecting overheating allegations involving its most powerful new smartphone processor, as questions grow over whether Samsung will use the chip in its Galaxy S27 Ultra.
On October 17, Qualcomm rejected reports of thermal problems with the Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6. The response followed South Korean reporting that Samsung had encountered performance slowdowns while testing the processor and was considering its Exynos 2700 chip as an alternative.
Samsung has not confirmed the alleged findings or announced a processor change. The dispute leaves questions about how Qualcomm’s new flagship chip will perform under sustained workloads in finished phones.
Qualcomm disputes Samsung testing allegations
The allegations originated in an October 16 Seoul Economic Daily report, which cited industry sources claiming Samsung’s internal tests found excessive temperatures and repeated performance slowdowns during demanding workloads.
Samsung reportedly requested improvements from Qualcomm and was weighing the Exynos 2700 if the Snapdragon processor failed to meet its requirements. Subsequent reporting indicated discussions could continue through the end of October.
Qualcomm rejected the allegations in a statement to 9to5Google, describing reports of thermal problems involving the Extreme chip as “inaccurate.”
Chief Marketing Officer Don McGuire separately wrote on X that there were “no systemic thermal issues” with the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6. He added that manufacturers routinely adjust performance and power consumption during device development.
McGuire did not explicitly identify the Extreme variant in his remarks, an ambiguity highlighted by Android Authority on October 19. Qualcomm’s separate statement addressed that processor directly, but neither company has publicly released data establishing whether the alleged problems occurred.
Qualcomm’s official specifications list a 2-nanometer manufacturing process and CPU speeds reaching 5GHz. Those figures describe the processor’s capabilities, not how consistently finished devices can maintain peak performance.
Qualcomm also introduced a standard Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6, with its features detailed in a separate platform overview. Samsung has not announced plans to replace Snapdragon in its Galaxy S27 Ultra.
Thermal throttling reduces processor speeds as temperatures rise. Although normal in modern chips, excessive throttling can disrupt demanding workloads, including gaming, prolonged video recording and on-device AI processing.
Peak benchmark scores cannot establish sustained performance on their own. Cooling hardware, battery capacity and software tuning also influence how individual smartphones manage heat.
Motorola’s upcoming Signature 27 flagship will feature the Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 and an ArcticMesh cooling system designed to sustain performance under load. Whether that design delivers consistent results will require independent testing.
Organizations evaluating Snapdragon-powered phones should compare performance, battery behavior and temperatures during repeated workloads rather than relying on brief benchmarks. Software support and management capabilities, including Android Enterprise AI controls, also factor into device procurement.
Qualcomm maintains that the overheating reports are inaccurate, while Samsung’s processor decision remains unconfirmed. Independent testing of shipping devices will be the clearest measure of whether the alleged thermal concerns translate into real-world performance limitations.

Qualcomm (NASDAQ:QCOM) trades at $176.86. Qualcomm has transformed itself from a smartphone chip supplier into an AI and data center company in a single investor cycle, and the market is still deciding whether to pay for that change.
Qualcomm sells Snapdragon processors through its QCT segment and licenses wireless patents through QTL. Its fiscal third quarter showed both sides of the business. Handset revenue fell 20% YoY to $5.09B, while automotive revenue rose 61% to $1.59B. Non-GAAP EPS of $2.21 came in just below the $2.22 estimate, which ended a six-quarter beat run. The stock trades 31% below its 52-week high of $257.56.
AI Pivot Doubles Qualcomm's Non-Handset Target
Management raised its fiscal 2029 non-handset revenue target to $40 billion from $22 billion. That figure includes more than $15 billion in data center revenue. Two custom silicon projects with global-scale hyperscalers start producing revenue in the December quarter, and purchase orders are already in place. Non-handset growth is expected to speed up from 24% in FY2026 to above 60% in FY2027.
Automotive has posted 23 consecutive quarters of double-digit growth, and BMW has named Qualcomm its lead compute supplier. Even so, the stock trades at a forward P/E of about 20, with a PEG ratio of 0.88 and a free cash flow yield near 6.79%.

Shrinking Handset Sales and Rising Costs Weigh on Qualcomm
The turn toward AI is costing a lot up front. Operating income fell 41.13% YoY as Qualcomm paid for the Modular and Alphawave acquisitions and its data center roadmap. Custom-chip revenue will also lower QCT gross margin by 1.5% to 2%. Meanwhile, the core business keeps shrinking. Qualcomm's chips will appear in a much smaller share of new iPhones, and revenue from Apple (NASDAQ:AAPL) is expected to fall about 50% from the September quarter to the December quarter. Weakness in Android is expected to reduce EPS by more than $1.50.
Chief executive Cristiano Amon acknowledged the doubt directly: "investors want to see more proof points that we can successfully execute on our plans as a new entrant."
Price Increases and December Data Center Revenue Will Decide the Next Move
Qualcomm is raising prices by double-digit percentages to offset higher memory, wafer and packaging costs. Management expects QCT gross margin to return to 48% to 50% as those increases take effect. Revenue from Chinese handset makers bottomed in the June quarter. Big funds are split: 6 tracked filers added shares, 4 cut and 2 sold out entirely.

December Data Center Revenue Is Qualcomm's Key Test
At $176.86, Qualcomm's outlook depends on execution.
The current price already reflects a lot of handset weakness, but Qualcomm has not yet shown it can earn money in AI. The first test is the December quarter, when hyperscaler revenue should start to come in. Management expects revenue to rise slightly from the prior quarter in that period, even with Apple revenue falling. All of that data center expansion has to be powered, cooled, and networked by somebody, and we rounded up seven suppliers riding the same wave in a free AI infrastructure report.
A stronger outlook would need two things: QCT margins returning to the 48% to 50% range, and data center revenue tracking toward the $5 billion fiscal 2027 goal. Intel and Qualcomm both showed up to earnings with a fresh AI identity, but investors have been voting with their feet ever since. One company is already cashing AI checks while the other is asking you to fund a roadmap…
Published October 14, 2026, 10:45am ET · 3 min read

Intel (NASDAQ:INTC | INTC Price Prediction) and Qualcomm (NASDAQ:QCOM) each used their summer earnings reports to sell investors on an AI identity. Intel highlighted server CPUs, advanced packaging and foundry capacity. Qualcomm highlighted cars, custom silicon and a data center plan that has not yet booked its first revenue. Since those reports, investors have cooled on both stories.
Intel closed at $102.81, just under the $103.79 it traded at when it reported. It also fell 8.61% this week. After a 178.62% year-to-date run, the pivot looks priced in. Qualcomm is up only 5.03% this year, which is a weak verdict.
Xeon Lifts Intel While Phones Sink Qualcomm
Intel’s revenue rose 25.4% to $16.13 billion, its strongest growth in more than 15 years. Data Center and AI led the way, jumping 59% on Xeon demand from hyperscale and enterprise customers. CEO Lip-Bu Tan said “strong demand for our products continues to outpace our growing supply.” CFO David Zinsner called the client gains “largely ASP,” meaning price increases and product mix did the lifting.
Qualcomm’s revenue slipped 4.0% to $9.95 billion. Handsets fell 20% as memory inflation hit phone makers. Its share of upcoming iPhones will also land well below its earlier 20% estimate. Automotive climbed 61% to a record $1.59 billion. EPS of $2.21 just missed the $2.22 estimate, ending a six-quarter streak of beats.
Android and Apple (NASDAQ:AAPL) handsets
Intel’s AI case rests on products it already ships: x86 CPUs, EMIB-T packaging with a “growing EMIB-T backlog,” and 18A plants. Capital spending for 2026 now tops $20 billion. Foundry is the soft spot. It lost $2.1 billion on just $293 million of external revenue.
Qualcomm is asking investors to pay for a future. Management raised its fiscal 2029 non-handset target to $40 billion, including $15 billion from data center. Custom chips for two hyperscalers start producing revenue in the December quarter, and a September collaboration with Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN) adds weight. However, those chips will initially cut QCT gross margin by 1.5% to 2%. CEO Cristiano Amon admitted that “investors want to see more proof points.”
Silicon Proof Will Decide Who Breaks Out
I am watching whether Intel’s 14A PDK 0.9, due in October, wins signed external foundry customers. For Qualcomm, keep an eye on its HBC silicon demonstration ahead of a mid-2027 launch. Also watch whether its double-digit price increases restore the historical 48% to 50% gross margin range.
Why I Lean Toward Intel’s Tangible AI Revenue
To me, Intel has the stronger AI evidence right now. AI-driven businesses generated roughly 70% of revenue, and the main constraint is supply. Still, the stock’s big run leaves little room if foundry struggles. Qualcomm’s case relies on automotive and a dividend raised to $0.92 to carry the business while data center grows. I would warm to Qualcomm once HBC performs on real silicon. Until then, Intel’s execution looks more solid to me (we reverse-engineered what the biggest AI chip winners looked like early and put the pattern in a free guide here: The Next Nvidia Playbook).

Through its planned acquisition of PickNik, Qualcomm Technologies aims to strengthen its robotics software portfolio and accelerate development on its Dragonwing platforms.
Qualcomm Technologies, Inc. announced its agreement to acquire PickNik Inc., an industry recognized robotics software company and longtime steward of MoveIt, one of the world's most widely adopted open-source robotics manipulation frameworks.
This acquisition is intended to strengthen Qualcomm Technologies' commitment to fostering an open robotics ecosystem, providing developers with the tools, software, and frameworks needed to move more efficiently from research and experimentation to prototyping, deployment, and production at scale.
In addition to remaining open-source, MoveIt is expected to offer streamlined integration with Dragonwing robotics platforms—providing developers with a more streamlined path from AI models such as VLAs and VLMs to planning, manipulation, and real-time control. The closing of this transaction is subject to customary closing conditions.
“Robotics is one of the most exciting frontiers of physical AI, and software is the connective tissue that turns great hardware into great robots,” said Nakul Duggal, EVP and Group GM, Automotive, Industrial and Embedded IoT, and Robotics, Qualcomm Technologies, Inc. “PickNik has earned tremendous trust within the global robotics community through its stewardship of MoveIt and its commitment to open-source innovation. Together, we plan to make it easier for developers to build advanced robotic applications on Dragonwing robotics platforms, while continuing to support the openness and collaboration that have made MoveIt successful.”
“Since our founding, PickNik’s mission has been to provide industries with a powerful, open platform that accelerates innovation and development of advanced robotics, well beyond traditional factories," said Dave Coleman, Founder and Chief Product Officer, PickNik Inc. “Joining Qualcomm Technologies will allow us to accelerate that mission, expand investment in MoveIt as a leading AI training platform for robotics, and deliver even more value to developers while preserving the openness, community collaboration, and cross-platform support that have always been central to our approach.”
“MoveIt is entering an exciting new chapter with the resources and support to help expand its impact,” said Dave Grant, Chief Executive Officer, PickNik Inc. “We look forward to joining Qualcomm Technologies and building on MoveIt’s momentum.”
Built atop the Robot Operating System (ROS), MoveIt has been used extensively by developers, students, researchers, and commercial robotics organizations worldwide to create sophisticated robotic applications in nearly every industry, including industrial automation, service robotics, mobile manipulation, and emerging physical AI systems.
Qualcomm Technologies and PickNik recognize that MoveIt’s value comes from its openness, broad adoption, and active developer community. Accordingly, Qualcomm Technologies intends for MoveIt to remain open-source under its existing license with community-driven roadmaps and open resources. Qualcomm Technologies also intends to continue supporting MoveIt across third-party hardware providers. MoveIt’s hardware-agnostic design is a key enabler of innovation, giving developers the freedom to choose the robot, compute platforms, and sensor components that best fit their needs.
Qualcomm Technologies and PickNik are both founding members of the Open Source Robotics Alliance (OSRA) and Qualcomm Technologies intends to continue driving major projects including Space ROS, a hardened version of ROS optimized for critical applications such as space exploration. Qualcomm Technologies will continue to support the open source development of MoveIt and ROS.
Accelerating Robotics Development on Dragonwing and Arduino
As part of the acquisition, MoveIt, MoveIt Pro — PickNik’s commercial platform designed to support advanced robotics systems — and future PickNik technologies, are poised to become more closely integrated with Dragonwing robotics platforms. This integration will enable developers to more easily take advantage of Dragonwing’s advanced AI, heterogeneous computing, connectivity, and real-time robotics capabilities in order to help simplify robotics development, shorten deployment timelines, and accelerate innovation across a broad range of robotic applications.
Developers building on Dragonwing should benefit from first-class, optimized support for MoveIt’s motion planning, manipulation, perception, and kinematics capabilities—helping to move from prototype to production faster while maintaining the flexibility to develop for diverse robotics architectures and deployment environments.
Starting with Arduino VENTUNO Q boards, MoveIt integration with Arduino aims to make advanced robotics, edge AI, and heterogeneous compute more accessible than ever. This integration seeks to extend powerful motion planning and autonomy capabilities to target millions of developers, helping shorten the journey from prototype to production-ready robots.
Qualcomm Technologies and PickNik displayed MoveIt Pro running on VENTUNO Q and Dragonwing robotics platforms last month at ROSCon Toronto.

Qualcomm plans to launch its first Wi-Fi 8 products by late 2026, enhancing network reliability, capacity, and latency with AI-powered gateways and advanced multi-antenna technology for improved connectivity.
The company is also working on network anomaly detection, troubleshooting and security applications. (Image/X)
Qualcomm is on track to bring its initial Wi-Fi 8 products to market towards the end of 2026, with the rollout expected to expand thereafter, according to a senior company executive.
Gautam Sheoran, Senior Vice President and General Manager, Connectivity, Broadband & Networking, Qualcomm told FE that the company is working with major OEM partners, including several existing Wi-Fi 7 partners, on the transition to Wi-Fi 8.

“Wi-Fi 8 is going to start at the end of this year with the most aggressive device makers, and then it’s going to expand in the next year,” he said.

Qualcomm is additionally integrating artificial intelligence engines into network gateways to classify applications and traffic, allowing networks to prioritise bandwidth and maintain quality of service for latency-sensitive applications. The company is also working on network anomaly detection, troubleshooting and security applications.
“Every house has a gateway that provides you internet access. And that’s typically been a black box or a white box, getting data in, sending data out, not a lot of intelligence,” Sheoran said, adding that this is an area where the company expects rapid change.
The shift towards intelligent gateways is particularly relevant as consumers use multiple connected devices simultaneously, mainly for cloud gaming, where delays in network response can affect the user experience.

The company has also worked on cutting power consumption, he added.
On top of this sits Qualcomm’s Dragonwing Network AI suite, which classifies traffic, applications and devices, Sheoran said that the firm seeks to develop in-home sensing and security features. “Edge security, especially in the gateways, is going to become more and more important,” Sheoran said, adding that hacking is getting easier.
India is major base for Qualcomm’s chip and software development, Sheoran said, calling the talent base and the volume of work as extremely integral.

Can Qualcomm's PickNik Acquisition Strengthen Its Robotics Edge?
Tue, October 20, 2026 at 8:09 AM CDT 2 min read
Qualcomm Incorporated QCOM is strengthening its position in the rapidly evolving robotics market through its proposed acquisition of PickNik Robotics, a developer of advanced robotics software. The transaction aligns with Qualcomm's strategy to expand its footprint in physical artificial intelligence (AI), edge computing and intelligent robotics.
PickNik is recognized for its stewardship of MoveIt, a widely adopted open-source robotics manipulation framework built on the Robot Operating System (ROS). The platform supports motion planning, manipulation and robotic control across industrial automation, service robotics and emerging physical AI applications. The transaction, subject to customary closing conditions, could strengthen Qualcomm's ability to offer integrated hardware and software solutions.
The buyout is expected to enhance Qualcomm's Dragonwing Robotics platforms by integrating MoveIt and PickNik's commercial MoveIt Pro software. This combination could enable developers to leverage Qualcomm's AI processing, connectivity and heterogeneous computing capabilities alongside advanced motion planning and real-time robotic control.
The integration is also expected to extend to Arduino platforms, beginning with VENTUNO Q boards. This could make advanced robotics development more accessible to a broader developer community while accelerating the transition from prototypes to commercial deployments.
Importantly, Qualcomm intends to maintain MoveIt as an open-source framework supporting third-party hardware. This approach could encourage wider ecosystem participation and strengthen developer engagement, potentially boosting adoption of its Dragonwing platforms.
Physical AI Opportunities Support Long-Term Diversification
The planned acquisition complements Qualcomm's broader efforts to diversify beyond smartphones into automotive, industrial IoT and edge AI markets. Its March 2026 collaboration with NEURA Robotics to advance cognitive robotics and humanoid applications further underscores its growing focus on physical AI.
Combining PickNik's software expertise with Qualcomm's power-efficient computing capabilities could improve its competitive positioning as demand for intelligent automation increases across industrial and commercial applications.
However, the acquisition's financial terms remain undisclosed, limiting visibility into its immediate earnings contribution. Integration challenges, competition in robotics computing and uncertain commercialization timelines could also constrain near-term benefits. Stiff competition from NVIDIA Corporation NVDA, Broadcom Inc. AVGO and Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. AMD further strains its margins.
Nevertheless, PickNik's established developer ecosystem and robotics software capabilities could help Qualcomm expand its addressable market and deepen customer engagement. Successful integration may strengthen QCOM's position in next-generation robotics while supporting its long-term diversification strategy.

Qualcomm Pushes Back on Snapdragon Overheating Reports Tied to Galaxy S27 Ultra
Qualcomm rejects Snapdragon overheating claims amid reports of Samsung testing problems, raising questions about the Galaxy S27 Ultra’s processor.
Qualcomm has rejected overheating allegations involving its Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 processor as questions persist about Samsung's Galaxy S27 Ultra chip choice. Image: Qualcomm Technologies, Inc.

Qualcomm is rejecting overheating allegations involving its most powerful new smartphone processor, as questions grow over whether Samsung will use the chip in its Galaxy S27 Ultra.
On October 17, Qualcomm rejected reports of thermal problems with the Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6. The response followed South Korean reporting that Samsung had encountered performance slowdowns while testing the processor and was considering its Exynos 2700 chip as an alternative.
Samsung has not confirmed the alleged findings or announced a processor change. The dispute leaves questions about how Qualcomm’s new flagship chip will perform under sustained workloads in finished phones.
Qualcomm disputes Samsung testing allegations
The allegations originated in an October 16 Seoul Economic Daily report, which cited industry sources claiming Samsung’s internal tests found excessive temperatures and repeated performance slowdowns during demanding workloads.
Samsung reportedly requested improvements from Qualcomm and was weighing the Exynos 2700 if the Snapdragon processor failed to meet its requirements. Subsequent reporting indicated discussions could continue through the end of October.
Qualcomm rejected the allegations in a statement to 9to5Google, describing reports of thermal problems involving the Extreme chip as “inaccurate.”
Chief Marketing Officer Don McGuire separately wrote on X that there were “no systemic thermal issues” with the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6. He added that manufacturers routinely adjust performance and power consumption during device development.
McGuire did not explicitly identify the Extreme variant in his remarks, an ambiguity highlighted by Android Authority on October 19. Qualcomm’s separate statement addressed that processor directly, but neither company has publicly released data establishing whether the alleged problems occurred.
Qualcomm’s official specifications list a 2-nanometer manufacturing process and CPU speeds reaching 5GHz. Those figures describe the processor’s capabilities, not how consistently finished devices can maintain peak performance.
Qualcomm also introduced a standard Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6, with its features detailed in a separate platform overview. Samsung has not announced plans to replace Snapdragon in its Galaxy S27 Ultra.
Thermal throttling reduces processor speeds as temperatures rise. Although normal in modern chips, excessive throttling can disrupt demanding workloads, including gaming, prolonged video recording and on-device AI processing.
Peak benchmark scores cannot establish sustained performance on their own. Cooling hardware, battery capacity and software tuning also influence how individual smartphones manage heat.
Motorola’s upcoming Signature 27 flagship will feature the Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 and an ArcticMesh cooling system designed to sustain performance under load. Whether that design delivers consistent results will require independent testing.
Organizations evaluating Snapdragon-powered phones should compare performance, battery behavior and temperatures during repeated workloads rather than relying on brief benchmarks. Software support and management capabilities, including Android Enterprise AI controls, also factor into device procurement.
Qualcomm maintains that the overheating reports are inaccurate, while Samsung’s processor decision remains unconfirmed. Independent testing of shipping devices will be the clearest measure of whether the alleged thermal concerns translate into real-world performance limitations.

QCOM doubled its non-handset revenue target to $40B by 2029, yet the stock sits 31% below its 52-week high as AI execution remains unproven.
Apple revenue is expected to drop 50% quarter-over-quarter while Android weakness threatens to cut QCOM EPS by more than $1.50.
23 of 37 analysts rate QCOM a Hold with a $194 average target, making the December hyperscaler revenue ramp the decisive proof point.
Just released. Our analysts combed the entire stock market and named the ten best stocks to buy right now, and Qualcomm didn't make the cut. Enter your email to see the names that beat QCOM. The report is free. Enter your email and see if any of your stocks made the cut.
Qualcomm (NASDAQ:QCOM) trades at $176.86. Qualcomm has transformed itself from a smartphone chip supplier into an AI and data center company in a single investor cycle, and the market is still deciding whether to pay for that change.
Qualcomm sells Snapdragon processors through its QCT segment and licenses wireless patents through QTL. Its fiscal third quarter showed both sides of the business. Handset revenue fell 20% YoY to $5.09B, while automotive revenue rose 61% to $1.59B. Non-GAAP EPS of $2.21 came in just below the $2.22 estimate, which ended a six-quarter beat run. The stock trades 31% below its 52-week high of $257.56.
AI Pivot Doubles Qualcomm's Non-Handset Target
Management raised its fiscal 2029 non-handset revenue target to $40 billion from $22 billion. That figure includes more than $15 billion in data center revenue. Two custom silicon projects with global-scale hyperscalers start producing revenue in the December quarter, and purchase orders are already in place. Non-handset growth is expected to speed up from 24% in FY2026 to above 60% in FY2027.
Automotive has posted 23 consecutive quarters of double-digit growth, and BMW has named Qualcomm its lead compute supplier. Even so, the stock trades at a forward P/E of about 20, with a PEG ratio of 0.88 and a free cash flow yield near 6.79%.
Why Didn't QCOM Make The Top 10 List?
24/7 Wall St has helped investors make money for over two decades, and our top analysts just finished ranking the definitive Top 10 Stocks To Buy Now. Not the ten biggest companies. Not the ten everyone is arguing about. The ten best stocks to buy right now.
And QCOM didn't make the cut!
The report is free, and you can see why we think each stock is a top investment today.
Shrinking Handset Sales and Rising Costs Weigh on Qualcomm
The turn toward AI is costing a lot up front. Operating income fell 41.13% YoY as Qualcomm paid for the Modular and Alphawave acquisitions and its data center roadmap. Custom-chip revenue will also lower QCT gross margin by 1.5% to 2%. Meanwhile, the core business keeps shrinking. Qualcomm's chips will appear in a much smaller share of new iPhones, and revenue from Apple (NASDAQ:AAPL) is expected to fall about 50% from the September quarter to the December quarter. Weakness in Android is expected to reduce EPS by more than $1.50.
Chief executive Cristiano Amon acknowledged the doubt directly: "investors want to see more proof points that we can successfully execute on our plans as a new entrant."
Price Increases and December Data Center Revenue Will Decide the Next Move
Qualcomm is raising prices by double-digit percentages to offset higher memory, wafer and packaging costs. Management expects QCT gross margin to return to 48% to 50% as those increases take effect. Revenue from Chinese handset makers bottomed in the June quarter. Big funds are split: 6 tracked filers added shares, 4 cut and 2 sold out entirely.
Most Analysts Rate It Hold, With a $194 Average Target
The average analyst target of $194.13 implies about 9.8% upside. Analyst targets are estimates and can change. Here is how the 37 analysts covering the stock rate it:
Qualcomm is up 5.03% year to date, compared with 14.1% for the S&P 500. Over one year, Qualcomm gained 11.62% while the index rose 17.35%.
December Data Center Revenue Is Qualcomm's Key Test
At $176.86, Qualcomm's outlook depends on execution.
The current price already reflects a lot of handset weakness, but Qualcomm has not yet shown it can earn money in AI. The first test is the December quarter, when hyperscaler revenue should start to come in. Management expects revenue to rise slightly from the prior quarter in that period, even with Apple revenue falling. All of that data center expansion has to be powered, cooled, and networked by somebody, and we rounded up seven suppliers riding the same wave in a free AI infrastructure report.
A stronger outlook would need two things: QCT margins returning to the 48% to 50% range, and data center revenue tracking toward the $5 billion fiscal 2027 goal. Android staying weak beyond the price increases or a slip in the custom silicon ramp would weaken the outlook. The 2.05% dividend yield provides income in the meantime.
The December quarter will show whether Qualcomm's AI plan produces revenue.

Qualcomm Vs. Intel: The Market is Refuting Both AI Rebrand Attempts
Intel and Qualcomm both showed up to earnings with a fresh AI identity, but investors have been voting with their feet ever since. One company is already cashing AI checks while the other is asking you to fund a roadmap…
Published October 14, 2026, 10:45am ET · 3 min read
This image visualizes the intricate connection between artificial intelligence, robotics, and market performance, reflecting the ongoing debate about Tesla's evolution into a leading AI firm. © Summit Art Creations / Shutterstock.com
Intel (NASDAQ:INTC | INTC Price Prediction) and Qualcomm (NASDAQ:QCOM) each used their summer earnings reports to sell investors on an AI identity. Intel highlighted server CPUs, advanced packaging and foundry capacity. Qualcomm highlighted cars, custom silicon and a data center plan that has not yet booked its first revenue. Since those reports, investors have cooled on both stories.
Intel closed at $102.81, just under the $103.79 it traded at when it reported. It also fell 8.61% this week. After a 178.62% year-to-date run, the pivot looks priced in. Qualcomm is up only 5.03% this year, which is a weak verdict.
Xeon Lifts Intel While Phones Sink Qualcomm
Intel’s revenue rose 25.4% to $16.13 billion, its strongest growth in more than 15 years. Data Center and AI led the way, jumping 59% on Xeon demand from hyperscale and enterprise customers. CEO Lip-Bu Tan said “strong demand for our products continues to outpace our growing supply.” CFO David Zinsner called the client gains “largely ASP,” meaning price increases and product mix did the lifting.
Qualcomm’s revenue slipped 4.0% to $9.95 billion. Handsets fell 20% as memory inflation hit phone makers. Its share of upcoming iPhones will also land well below its earlier 20% estimate. Automotive climbed 61% to a record $1.59 billion. EPS of $2.21 just missed the $2.22 estimate, ending a six-quarter streak of beats.
Android and Apple (NASDAQ:AAPL) handsets
Intel’s AI case rests on products it already ships: x86 CPUs, EMIB-T packaging with a “growing EMIB-T backlog,” and 18A plants. Capital spending for 2026 now tops $20 billion. Foundry is the soft spot. It lost $2.1 billion on just $293 million of external revenue.
Qualcomm is asking investors to pay for a future. Management raised its fiscal 2029 non-handset target to $40 billion, including $15 billion from data center. Custom chips for two hyperscalers start producing revenue in the December quarter, and a September collaboration with Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN) adds weight. However, those chips will initially cut QCT gross margin by 1.5% to 2%. CEO Cristiano Amon admitted that “investors want to see more proof points.”
Silicon Proof Will Decide Who Breaks Out
I am watching whether Intel’s 14A PDK 0.9, due in October, wins signed external foundry customers. For Qualcomm, keep an eye on its HBC silicon demonstration ahead of a mid-2027 launch. Also watch whether its double-digit price increases restore the historical 48% to 50% gross margin range.
Why I Lean Toward Intel’s Tangible AI Revenue
To me, Intel has the stronger AI evidence right now. AI-driven businesses generated roughly 70% of revenue, and the main constraint is supply. Still, the stock’s big run leaves little room if foundry struggles. Qualcomm’s case relies on automotive and a dividend raised to $0.92 to carry the business while data center grows. I would warm to Qualcomm once HBC performs on real silicon. Until then, Intel’s execution looks more solid to me (we reverse-engineered what the biggest AI chip winners looked like early and put the pattern in a free guide here: The Next Nvidia Playbook).

Through its planned acquisition of PickNik, Qualcomm Technologies aims to strengthen its robotics software portfolio and accelerate development on its Dragonwing platforms.
Through its planned acquisition of PickNik, Qualcomm Technologies aims to strengthen its robotics software portfolio and accelerate development on its Dragonwing platforms.
Qualcomm Technologies, Inc. announced its agreement to acquire PickNik Inc., an industry recognized robotics software company and longtime steward of MoveIt, one of the world's most widely adopted open-source robotics manipulation frameworks.
This acquisition is intended to strengthen Qualcomm Technologies' commitment to fostering an open robotics ecosystem, providing developers with the tools, software, and frameworks needed to move more efficiently from research and experimentation to prototyping, deployment, and production at scale.
In addition to remaining open-source, MoveIt is expected to offer streamlined integration with Dragonwing robotics platforms—providing developers with a more streamlined path from AI models such as VLAs and VLMs to planning, manipulation, and real-time control. The closing of this transaction is subject to customary closing conditions.
“Robotics is one of the most exciting frontiers of physical AI, and software is the connective tissue that turns great hardware into great robots,” said Nakul Duggal, EVP and Group GM, Automotive, Industrial and Embedded IoT, and Robotics, Qualcomm Technologies, Inc. “PickNik has earned tremendous trust within the global robotics community through its stewardship of MoveIt and its commitment to open-source innovation. Together, we plan to make it easier for developers to build advanced robotic applications on Dragonwing robotics platforms, while continuing to support the openness and collaboration that have made MoveIt successful.”
“Since our founding, PickNik’s mission has been to provide industries with a powerful, open platform that accelerates innovation and development of advanced robotics, well beyond traditional factories," said Dave Coleman, Founder and Chief Product Officer, PickNik Inc. “Joining Qualcomm Technologies will allow us to accelerate that mission, expand investment in MoveIt as a leading AI training platform for robotics, and deliver even more value to developers while preserving the openness, community collaboration, and cross-platform support that have always been central to our approach.”
“MoveIt is entering an exciting new chapter with the resources and support to help expand its impact,” said Dave Grant, Chief Executive Officer, PickNik Inc. “We look forward to joining Qualcomm Technologies and building on MoveIt’s momentum.”
Built atop the Robot Operating System (ROS), MoveIt has been used extensively by developers, students, researchers, and commercial robotics organizations worldwide to create sophisticated robotic applications in nearly every industry, including industrial automation, service robotics, mobile manipulation, and emerging physical AI systems.
Qualcomm Technologies and PickNik recognize that MoveIt’s value comes from its openness, broad adoption, and active developer community. Accordingly, Qualcomm Technologies intends for MoveIt to remain open-source under its existing license with community-driven roadmaps and open resources. Qualcomm Technologies also intends to continue supporting MoveIt across third-party hardware providers. MoveIt’s hardware-agnostic design is a key enabler of innovation, giving developers the freedom to choose the robot, compute platforms, and sensor components that best fit their needs.
Qualcomm Technologies and PickNik are both founding members of the Open Source Robotics Alliance (OSRA) and Qualcomm Technologies intends to continue driving major projects including Space ROS, a hardened version of ROS optimized for critical applications such as space exploration. Qualcomm Technologies will continue to support the open source development of MoveIt and ROS.
Accelerating Robotics Development on Dragonwing and Arduino
As part of the acquisition, MoveIt, MoveIt Pro — PickNik’s commercial platform designed to support advanced robotics systems — and future PickNik technologies, are poised to become more closely integrated with Dragonwing robotics platforms. This integration will enable developers to more easily take advantage of Dragonwing’s advanced AI, heterogeneous computing, connectivity, and real-time robotics capabilities in order to help simplify robotics development, shorten deployment timelines, and accelerate innovation across a broad range of robotic applications.
Developers building on Dragonwing should benefit from first-class, optimized support for MoveIt’s motion planning, manipulation, perception, and kinematics capabilities—helping to move from prototype to production faster while maintaining the flexibility to develop for diverse robotics architectures and deployment environments.
Starting with Arduino VENTUNO Q boards, MoveIt integration with Arduino aims to make advanced robotics, edge AI, and heterogeneous compute more accessible than ever. This integration seeks to extend powerful motion planning and autonomy capabilities to target millions of developers, helping shorten the journey from prototype to production-ready robots.
Qualcomm Technologies and PickNik displayed MoveIt Pro running on VENTUNO Q and Dragonwing robotics platforms last month at ROSCon Toronto.

Qualcomm wins lawsuit against Arm but will only receive two bucks
Arm accuses Qualcomm of filing the lawsuit to get out of paying ‘billions of dollars’ in royalties
Add Engadget on Google:
Both Arm and Qualcomm have published statements, saying that they were pleased with the findings of a Delaware jury in a breach of licensing lawsuit. That's because while the jury found that Arm breached its Architectural License Agreement with Qualcomm and acted to disrupt its business, it also only awarded the latter company a total of $2 in damages. Yes, just $2 — that figure isn't missing a million or a billion.
The two companies have been embroiled in legal battles for years. In 2022, Arm sued Qualcomm after the latter purchased Nuvia, which also licenses its technologies. Arm had argued at the time that Qualcomm didn't obtain the necessary permits to transfer Nuvia's licenses, constituting a breach of contract. Last year, Qualcomm announced that the court had granted it "complete victory" after it dismissed Arm's remaining claims.
According to Thurrott, due to the information that emerged during that case's discovery and the things Arm Holdings CEO Rene Haas' said on the stand, Qualcomm sued Arm. Reuters says that after a five-day trial, the jury found that Arm had breached their agreements by withholding software patches and tools for its designs. It also found that Arm intentionally interfered with Qualcomm's business deal with Meta. Qualcomm alleged that in 2024, Arm had leaked to Bloomberg News that it had breached a licensing agreement when it was on the verge of closing a deal with Meta, leading to a delay. The jury sided with Arm in four of Qualcomm's other claims.
In its statement, Arm said the lawsuit was an attempt by Qualcomm to get out of paying it "billions of dollars" under the companies' existing licensing agreements.
"We are pleased with the jury' decision today finding for Arm on four claims and awarding only one dollar in damages on each of Qualcomm's other two claims," Arm said. "Despite Qualcomm's pursuit of this case in an attempt to deprive Arm of billions of dollars under our license agreements, the jury's verdict confirms that Arm operated in good faith under its technology license agreement and its award of only two dollars confirms the merit of Arm's arguments in the case."
Meanwhile, Qualcomm said it was "gratified that the jury found Arm breached its long-standing Architectural License Agreement (ALA) with Qualcomm, failed to honor its commitments, and intentionally acted to disrupt Qualcomm's businesses." It added: "Together with Qualcomm's prior court victory, this outcome further exposes Arm's broader intentions to harm Qualcomm and its ecosystem."
Their court battle, however, is far from over. US District Judge ​Maryellen Noreika is still expected to resolve several more disputes between the companies. If Noreika ultimately sides with Qualcomm, the company could stop paying Arm royalties for five years, which as Arm said was worth billions of dollars. Arm argued that the penalty, as indicated in the companies' licensing contract, isn't enforceable.

Qualcomm on track to bring first Wi-Fi 8 products to market by end-2026
Qualcomm plans to launch its first Wi-Fi 8 products by late 2026, enhancing network reliability, capacity, and latency with AI-powered gateways and advanced multi-antenna technology for improved connectivity.
The company is also working on network anomaly detection, troubleshooting and security applications. (Image/X)
Qualcomm is on track to bring its initial Wi-Fi 8 products to market towards the end of 2026, with the rollout expected to expand thereafter, according to a senior company executive.
Gautam Sheoran, Senior Vice President and General Manager, Connectivity, Broadband & Networking, Qualcomm told FE that the company is working with major OEM partners, including several existing Wi-Fi 7 partners, on the transition to Wi-Fi 8.
Trai allows two-way communication on 1600 series
“Wi-Fi 8 is going to start at the end of this year with the most aggressive device makers, and then it’s going to expand in the next year,” he said.
The technology is designed to improve network reliability, increase capacity and reduce latency, particularly as connected devices increasingly support simultaneous applications such as gaming, video streaming, remote work and Internet of Things (IoT) services.
Qualcomm is additionally integrating artificial intelligence engines into network gateways to classify applications and traffic, allowing networks to prioritise bandwidth and maintain quality of service for latency-sensitive applications. The company is also working on network anomaly detection, troubleshooting and security applications.
“Every house has a gateway that provides you internet access. And that’s typically been a black box or a white box, getting data in, sending data out, not a lot of intelligence,” Sheoran said, adding that this is an area where the company expects rapid change.
The shift towards intelligent gateways is particularly relevant as consumers use multiple connected devices simultaneously, mainly for cloud gaming, where delays in network response can affect the user experience.
Imprint of price rejig, user churn likely on telcos quarter
Sheoran added that for the first time, Qualcomm is putting a 4×4 Wi-Fi radio in its handset chips. It is also launching what it calls the industry’s first 5×5 radio for access points. The extra antennas extend range and improve stability. The chips integrate AI engines that prioritise traffic, so that gaming, work calls and streaming do not compete in busy homes. The company has also worked on cutting power consumption, he added.
On top of this sits Qualcomm’s Dragonwing Network AI suite, which classifies traffic, applications and devices, Sheoran said that the firm seeks to develop in-home sensing and security features. “Edge security, especially in the gateways, is going to become more and more important,” Sheoran said, adding that hacking is getting easier.
India is major base for Qualcomm’s chip and software development, Sheoran said, calling the talent base and the volume of work as extremely integral.

Can Qualcomm's PickNik Acquisition Strengthen Its Robotics Edge?
Tue, October 20, 2026 at 8:09 AM CDT 2 min read
Qualcomm Incorporated QCOM is strengthening its position in the rapidly evolving robotics market through its proposed acquisition of PickNik Robotics, a developer of advanced robotics software. The transaction aligns with Qualcomm's strategy to expand its footprint in physical artificial intelligence (AI), edge computing and intelligent robotics.
PickNik is recognized for its stewardship of MoveIt, a widely adopted open-source robotics manipulation framework built on the Robot Operating System (ROS). The platform supports motion planning, manipulation and robotic control across industrial automation, service robotics and emerging physical AI applications. The transaction, subject to customary closing conditions, could strengthen Qualcomm's ability to offer integrated hardware and software solutions.
The buyout is expected to enhance Qualcomm's Dragonwing Robotics platforms by integrating MoveIt and PickNik's commercial MoveIt Pro software. This combination could enable developers to leverage Qualcomm's AI processing, connectivity and heterogeneous computing capabilities alongside advanced motion planning and real-time robotic control.
The integration is also expected to extend to Arduino platforms, beginning with VENTUNO Q boards. This could make advanced robotics development more accessible to a broader developer community while accelerating the transition from prototypes to commercial deployments.
Importantly, Qualcomm intends to maintain MoveIt as an open-source framework supporting third-party hardware. This approach could encourage wider ecosystem participation and strengthen developer engagement, potentially boosting adoption of its Dragonwing platforms.
Physical AI Opportunities Support Long-Term Diversification
The planned acquisition complements Qualcomm's broader efforts to diversify beyond smartphones into automotive, industrial IoT and edge AI markets. Its March 2026 collaboration with NEURA Robotics to advance cognitive robotics and humanoid applications further underscores its growing focus on physical AI.
Combining PickNik's software expertise with Qualcomm's power-efficient computing capabilities could improve its competitive positioning as demand for intelligent automation increases across industrial and commercial applications.
However, the acquisition's financial terms remain undisclosed, limiting visibility into its immediate earnings contribution. Integration challenges, competition in robotics computing and uncertain commercialization timelines could also constrain near-term benefits. Stiff competition from NVIDIA Corporation NVDA, Broadcom Inc. AVGO and Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. AMD further strains its margins.
Nevertheless, PickNik's established developer ecosystem and robotics software capabilities could help Qualcomm expand its addressable market and deepen customer engagement. Successful integration may strengthen QCOM's position in next-generation robotics while supporting its long-term diversification strategy.

Prediction: Qualcomm Could Be on the Verge of a Major Transformation
Qualcomm is entering data center and automotive markets at full speed while Apple shrinks its handset business and analysts pile on with downward revisions. Whether those new revenue streams arrive fast enough to fill the gap will decide everything for…
Published October 5, 2026, 8:45am ET · 3 min read
Price Targets desk. Editor: Vandita Jadeja.
The 24/7 Wall St. price target for Qualcomm (NASDAQ:QCOM | QCOM Price Prediction) is $218.04 over the next 12 months. From a reference price of $184.1, that works out to 18.44% upside, and our model rates the stock a buy.
Price Target from 24/7 Wall St.
Management targets $40 billion in non-handset revenue by fiscal 2029, up from $22 billion. Non-handset growth is expected to speed up from 24% in fiscal 2026 to greater than 60% in fiscal 2027. If Qualcomm delivers, the business will look very different by decade’s end.
Qualcomm Has Pulled Back Hard From Its June Peak
The stock is down 6.01% over the past week. It is still up 14.12% over the past month and 10.67% year to date. Qualcomm underperformed its competitors on Monday. Shares trade about 28.5% below their 52-week high of $257.56 and about 52.3% above their low of $120.88.
In fiscal Q3, revenue came in at $9.947 billion, ahead of the $9.672 billion estimate. Non-GAAP EPS of $2.21 narrowly missed expectations. Handset revenue fell 20%, while automotive revenue rose 61% to $1.588 billion.
Why Bulls See Data Center Revenue Rewriting the Story
Two custom silicon deals with hyperscalers begin revenue in the December quarter. Management targets $5 billion in fiscal 2027 and $15 billion in fiscal 2029 for data center.
The AI expansion reaches well beyond the accelerator makers, and we featured seven of the less-obvious infrastructure suppliers in a free report you can grab here.
In automotive, Qualcomm raised its annualized revenue target to about $7 billion and won the lead compute supplier role for BMW’s next-generation ADAS and digital cockpit. The most optimistic fiscal 2027 EPS estimate is $12.24. Our bull case of $237.62 implies about 29% upside.
Apple’s Exit and Margin Pressure Could Stall the Rerating
Management expects Apple product revenue to fall about 50% from September to December. Over the past 30 days, analysts made 27 downward revisions to fiscal 2027 estimates.
Consensus EPS for fiscal 2027 now stands at $10.1772, below the $10.4834 expected for fiscal 2026. Custom data center chips could cut QCT gross margin by 1.5% to 2%.
Qualcomm is raising prices by double-digit amounts to offset higher costs. In the bear case of $185.27, the stock stays about flat over 12 months.
Qualcomm Trades Below Its Custom Silicon Rivals
Broadcom (NASDAQ:AVGO) leads the hyperscaler custom silicon market that Qualcomm is entering. It trades at nearly the same forward multiple while growing revenue 85.5%.
Marvell (NASDAQ:MRVL) shows what investors pay once a custom silicon ramp is proven: a forward multiple of 62x.
Texas Instruments (NASDAQ:TXN) is a useful comparison for automotive and industrial chips, and it trades at 28x. Against this group, the 24/7 Wall St. price target looks conservative.
Qualcomm’s Transformation Tips the Balance Toward Upside
The 24/7 Wall St. price target is $218.04, with a buy rating and 90% confidence. Qualcomm trades at a peer-level multiple while data center revenue is only now coming.
Upside hinges on hyperscaler shipments starting on schedule in December and price increases restoring margins. On the downside, Android weakness could compound the Apple decline.
These year-end targets assume Qualcomm keeps executing its current strategy.
Price Target from 24/7 Wall St.
The biggest swing factor is data center execution. Hitting the $15 billion fiscal 2029 target would push results above this path, and a delayed accelerator launch would pull them below it.

Qualcomm To Reportedly Conduct Global Layoffs In Performance-Driven Overhaul
Tue, October 20, 2026 at 1:07 PM CDT 2 min read
Qualcomm CEO Cristiano Amon announced the worldwide job cuts in an internal memo, with individual notifications scheduled to begin in November.
Although the exact magnitude of the layoffs has not been disclosed, the firm reported a global headcount of approximately 52,000 employees as of last September.
The downsizing coincides with ongoing consumer electronics slumps and a strategic corporate transition toward artificial intelligence data-center expansion.
Qualcomm (QCOM) is preparing to downsize its global workforce through a performance-focused reduction strategy, Reuters reported on Tuesday.
In an internal company memo reviewed by Reuters on Monday, Chief Executive Officer Cristiano Amon informed staff that the upcoming personnel changes will follow after the completion of yearly employee performance evaluations.

Amon stated that the workforce adjustments are designed to build a robust performance culture and directly address instances where teams have consistently missed targets.
While the memo omitted specific figures regarding the total number of positions affected, public records indicate that Qualcomm maintained roughly 52,000 full-time global employees as of September of last year. Formal notifications regarding the cuts are slated to begin rolling out in November.
Qualcomm is among the world's leading smartphone chipmakers and is facing significant headwinds lately from a broader demand slump driven by soaring memory component prices.
Consequently, Qualcomm shares have experienced sluggish growth, rising just 1.5% in 2026, lagging significantly behind the broader S&P 500 and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index (SOX).
Amon emphasized that the restructuring process will carefully weigh current business priorities, required organizational competencies, and individual skill sets. "As we have expanded the business, so have the competencies and skills we require," Amon noted in the internal communication. "We must have the right people in the right roles so they can perform at their best and the company can continue to succeed."

Qualcomm stock (ISIN US7475251036) was trading at EUR 161.28 at Lang & Schwarz on October 6, 2026 at 10:15 a.m. CEST, down 0.19 percent versus the prior close of EUR 161.58. On October 5, 2026, Qualcomm and Huawei announced a multi-year patent agreement covering 5G, compute, artificial intelligence and networking.
According to Huawei on October 5, 2026, the companies will cross-license their patent portfolios, while Qualcomm will purchase certain Huawei U.S. patents covering compute, artificial intelligence, networking and other technologies.
The transaction remains subject to regulatory approvals, and the companies disclosed no financial terms. Reuters reported on October 5, 2026, that the agreement is Huawei's first patent licensing deal with Qualcomm covering 5G and could lift Huawei's cumulative licensing contract value above USD 6.9 billion once completed.
Qualcomm's latest reported quarter ended June 28, 2026. MarketBeat reported that third-quarter revenue reached USD 9.95 billion, down 4.00 percent from the same quarter of 2025, while earnings per share came to USD 2.21 against consensus of USD 2.23.
The comparison shows a mixed earnings profile. Revenue exceeded the USD 9.69 billion estimate cited by MarketBeat, but earnings per share missed consensus by USD 0.02, leaving the licensing agreement as a strategic development rather than a quantified near-term earnings boost.
The primary-market quote was last at USD 180.79 on Nasdaq at 4:00 p.m. ET on October 5, 2026. Qualcomm's market capitalization was USD 189.8 billion on that date, while its 52-week range stood at USD 121.99 to USD 259.92.
The valuation context matters because the Huawei agreement has no disclosed purchase price or royalty schedule. For Qualcomm, the immediate investor question is whether the added patents strengthen future compute and networking offerings while the handset business faces a year-over-year revenue decline.

"We are pleased to have reached this early renewal of Transsion's 4G and 5G licenses and to combine the existing 4G and 5G agreements into a single long-term agreement," said John Han, Executive Vice President and General Manager of Qualcomm Technology Licensing (QTL).
Qualcomm is a global computing leader at the center of the AI era, enabling intelligence to scale from the most personal devices to large-scale infrastructure. Building on more than four decades of innovation, we develop platforms and solutions that bring together advanced AI, high-performance, low-power computing and industry-leading connectivity-powering products and services used around the world. At Qualcomm, we are engineering human progress.
Qualcomm Incorporated includes our licensing business, QTL, and the vast majority of our patent portfolio. Texas Instruments (TXN) To Report Earnings Tomorrow: Here Is What To Expect
Analog chip manufacturer Texas Instruments (NASDAQ:TXN) will be announcing earnings results this Wednesday after the bell. Here's what you need to know.
Texas Instruments beat analysts' revenue expectations last quarter, reporting revenues of $5.46 billion, up 22.8% year on year. It was an exceptional quarter for the company, with a beat of analysts' EPS and operating income estimates.
Is Texas Instruments a buy or sell going into earnings? Read our full analysis here, it's free for active Edge members.
This quarter, the market is expecting Texas Instruments's revenue to grow 24.4% year on year, improving from the 14.2% increase it recorded in the same quarter last year.
Analysts covering the company have generally reconfirmed their estimates over the last 30 days, suggesting they anticipate the business will stay the course heading into earnings. Texas Instruments rarely misses Wall Street's revenue estimates.
Looking at Texas Instruments's peers in the semiconductors segment, some have already reported their Q3 results, giving us a hint as to what we can expect. Penguin Solutions delivered year-on-year revenue growth of 67.7%, beating analysts' expectations by 8.8%, and Micron reported revenues up 379%, topping estimates by 6.4%. Penguin Solutions traded up 13.1% following the results while Micron was also up 3%.
Read our full analysis of Penguin Solutions's results here and Micron's results here.
Over the last year or so, investors' attention has moved from one major market theme to the next, spanning AI disruption and surging infrastructure investment to geopolitical tensions, interest rates, and the health of the broader economy. While some of the semiconductors stocks have shown solid performance in this choppy environment, the group has generally underperformed, with share prices down 7.8% on average over the last month. Texas Instruments is up 2.5% during the same time and is heading into earnings with an average analyst price target of $324.39 (compared to the current share price of $277.56).

Lam Research and Texas Instruments both report after the close on Wednesday, and each faces a different kind of pressure: one must prove AI equipment demand is still accelerating, while the other needs to show its industrial recovery has real…
Published October 20, 2026, 7:50am ET · 3 min read
Automated robotic arms meticulously assemble electronic components on an advanced manufacturing line, illustrating the high-tech production methods driving growth in the semiconductor industry, particularly for AI equipment and industrial applications. © Shutterstock
Two chip stocks from opposite ends of the industry report on Wednesday, October 21, after the market close. Lam Research (NASDAQ:LRCX | LRCX Price Prediction) has to show that AI equipment demand is still accelerating. Texas Instruments (NASDAQ:TXN) has to show that its industrial and auto rebound can last.
Texas Instruments hosts its call at 3:30 p.m. Central time (4:30 p.m. ET). Lam follows at 5:00 p.m. ET.
Texas Instruments Faces a Test of Its Own Guidance
Texas Instruments makes analog chips that handle real-world signals like power and temperature. It also makes embedded processors, the small control chips built into machines. On its prior earnings call, Texas Instruments said revenue rose 13% sequentially and 23% year over year. Industrial, data center, and automotive customers led the growth.
Texas Instruments guided third-quarter revenue to $5.65 billion to $6.15 billion and EPS to $2.23 to $2.57. The consensus EPS estimate of $2.42 falls inside that range, so the fourth-quarter outlook carries more weight. Management said industrial revenue remains below its 2022 peak and customer inventories have not been rebuilt. Auto demand picked up, led by electric vehicles and hybrids in China. Shares are up 59.2% year to date.
Lam Research Rides AI Demand Into Record Guidance
Lam sells deposition and etch tools, the machines that add and carve away thin layers of material on silicon wafers. On its prior earnings call, Lam said it delivered record revenue, operating margin, and earnings per share “as AI-driven demand continues to reshape the semiconductor industry,” positioning it for “a third consecutive year of outperformance in 2026.”
Lam guided September-quarter revenue to $8.1 billion, plus or minus $400 million, and EPS to $2.15 plus or minus $0.15. It also raised its 2026 forecast for wafer fab equipment spending (what the whole industry spends on chipmaking tools) to the low $150 billion range.
In an August 26 Bloomberg Businessweek report, Lam Research said its advanced packaging business is growing more than 70% year over year. Advanced packaging stacks memory and processor chips in three dimensions and wires them together, so AI hardware works like one large system. Lam shares are down 12.1% over the past week and up 59.0% year to date.
Consensus Points to Steep Year-Over-Year Gains
Jim Cramer described the demand picture on October 19, saying CPUs are “going to be in very short supply, which I think is absolutely true because Taiwan Semi can’t make all the ones that they have.” He added, “There’s tremendous demand, and there’s also an inability to build.” On October 9, he said, “Taiwan Semi controlled pretty much any chip stock.”
When chipmakers cannot build fast enough, they add factory capacity, and that means buying more deposition and etch tools from Lam. Lam said the industry remains meaningfully undersupplied, with several new fabs expected to come online by the end of 2027. The same buildout is pulling in power, cooling, and networking suppliers alongside the chipmakers. (We rounded up seven of those names in a free AI infrastructure report.)
What Each Company Must Prove on Wednesday
Texas Instruments needs a fourth-quarter outlook showing that industrial and automotive demand is still climbing. Lam needs revenue close to its $8.1 billion guidance and more detail on 2027, a year management already called a potentially strong setup.

Texas Instruments Incorporated (US8825081040) stock is trading at EUR 244.18 at Lang & Schwarz on October 20, 2026 at 10:33 a.m. CEST. On October 19, 2026, StoneX reiterated a Buy rating and a USD 360.00 price target, according to Investing.com.

KeyCorp raised its third-quarter 2026 earnings-per-share forecast to USD 2.48 from USD 2.23 on October 14, 2026, and kept a USD 400.00 target, according to MarketBeat. That spread of targets shows why the coming report matters for valuation as well as operating results.
What does the USD 360.00 target mean?
The latest reported quarter provides the operating benchmark. Texas Instruments posted USD 5.46 billion of revenue and USD 2.14 diluted earnings per share for the second quarter of 2026, with revenue up 22.8 percent year over year, according to EarningsMadness. The company forecast third-quarter revenue of USD 5.65 billion to USD 6.15 billion, giving the October report a clear range against which to measure demand.
On July 22, 2026, Texas Instruments reported USD 5.46 billion in second-quarter revenue and USD 2.14 diluted earnings per share. On October 15, 2026, its board declared a quarterly dividend of USD 1.52 per share, up from USD 1.42, according to MarketBeat. On October 19, 2026, StoneX reiterated its USD 360.00 target and Buy rating.
Texas Instruments is scheduled to report third-quarter 2026 results on October 21, 2026, after the market close, with its earnings call set for 4:30 p.m. ET. October 30, 2026 is the stated record and ex-dividend date for the USD 1.52 quarterly payment, according to EarningsMadness.
